front_matter.purpose:
## Purpose

This Policy & Procedure Manual sets out how **[AGENCY NAME]** operates its Illinois assisted living or shared housing establishment. It is written for an establishment licensed by the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) under the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act (210 ILCS 9) and the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Establishment Code (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295). Where **[AGENCY NAME]** is also approved and certified by the Illinois Department of Healthcare and Family Services (HFS) for Medicaid payment through the Supportive Living Program, the manual also addresses 89 Ill. Adm. Code 146.

The manual is intended to:

- Turn state statutory and regulatory requirements into consistent, day-to-day practice for residents, staff, and management.
- Cover resident assessment, service planning, admission and retention, medication services, staffing and training, background checks, resident contracts, and dementia care.
- Give staff a reference for what to do, who is responsible, and what must be documented.
- Support readiness for IDPH licensure, renewal, and survey activity, and for HFS certification where it applies.
- Protect resident health, safety, dignity, and rights.

**This manual is a template and is not legal advice.** It is not complete or effective until **[AGENCY NAME]** customizes it, the governing body adopts it, and staff are trained on it (see *How to Use This Manual*).
front_matter.how_to_use:
## How to Use This Manual

### 1. Customize it before use
This manual contains **[AGENCY NAME]** placeholders and other bracketed fields, such as **[ADMINISTRATOR/DIRECTOR NAME]**, **[LICENSE NUMBER]**, **[PHYSICAL ADDRESS]**, and **[GOVERNING BODY]**. Replace every placeholder with facts specific to your establishment. Revise each policy so it reflects what **[AGENCY NAME]** actually does: your license type (assisted living or shared housing), standard or floating licensure, unit count, services offered, whether you operate a special dementia program, and whether you participate in the HFS Supportive Living Program. Delete or mark "not applicable" any content that does not fit your operation. For example, the Supportive Living Program content applies only if HFS has separately approved and certified the facility. It does not apply to a private-pay-only establishment.

### 2. Adopt it formally
After customization, the **[GOVERNING BODY]** of **[AGENCY NAME]** must review and formally adopt the manual. Record the adoption date, the approving individuals or body, and the version number on the adoption page: **[ADOPTION DATE]**, **[VERSION]**, **[SIGNATURES]**. Keep the signed adoption record with the master copy.

### 3. Keep it current
Statutes and rules change. The ILGA page for Public Act 104-0589 (HB 3392), which amends 210 ILCS 9/15, 35, 70, 135 and 150, shows an effective date of 7/24/2026, while Section 99 of the Act says it takes effect on becoming law. **Confirm the operative effective date with IDPH or legal counsel** before relying on the amended text. The LII version of 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000 shows its history as last amended in 2004, so check it against the current JCAR text. Assign **[ROLE/TITLE]** to review the manual at least annually and whenever a law, rule, IDPH or HFS guidance, or **[AGENCY NAME]** practice changes. Log each revision with its date and reason, replace superseded pages in every copy, and retain prior versions according to **[AGENCY NAME]**'s records policy.

### 4. Train staff on it
Staff must be trained on this manual, and training must be documented. Train each employee on the policies relevant to their role at hire and again when policies change. Document the date, content, trainer, and attendee signature or acknowledgment for each session, and keep the records in the employee file. Training required by law (for example, adult CPR for direct care staff, ongoing staff training, director training, and dementia training where applicable) is addressed in the personnel and dementia-care sections.

### 5. Use it day to day
- Make the manual available to all staff, and keep a current copy at **[LOCATION]**.
- Follow the cited rule when a policy and a rule appear to differ. The statute and regulation control over this manual. Raise the discrepancy with **[ROLE/TITLE]** so the manual can be corrected.
- Use the regulatory framework section to find the authority behind each policy.
- Do not rely on summaries of rules here as the full legal text. Read the full text of the cited rules, including 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2000 for the complete list of residency conditions.
- Report questions and suspected violations to **[ADMINISTRATOR/DIRECTOR NAME]** promptly.
front_matter.regulatory_framework:
## Regulatory Framework

The rules below are cited by their exact cite text. The summaries are brief and are **not substitutes for the full legal text**. Confirm current text with the source before relying on it.

### A. Statutes

- **210 ILCS 9/15**: Assessment and service plan requirements. A comprehensive pre-admission assessment of physical, cognitive, and psychosocial condition by a physician, physician assistant, or APRN. It is repeated at least annually and on a significant change in condition, including a diagnosis of Alzheimer's or a related dementia. A written service plan is mutually agreed by provider, resident, and representative, and reviewed at least annually or when needs change. On request, the resident or representative receives a copy of the latest assessment, any supplemental establishment assessment, and the service plan.
- **210 ILCS 9/25**: License requirement. No person may establish, operate, maintain, or offer an assisted living or shared housing establishment without a license.
- **210 ILCS 9/35**: Issuance of license. Director qualifications (21+, high school diploma or equivalent, qualifying experience). Staff sufficient in number and skill for 24-hour scheduled and unscheduled needs, with ongoing training. Health Care Worker Background Check Act compliance. Alzheimer's/dementia special care disclosure filing. A director must complete at least 20 hours of training every 2 years. Licenses last one year, state the physical location and dates, and are not transferable.
- **210 ILCS 9/45**: Renewal of licenses. Renewal applications are filed 120-150 days before expiration. IDPH may grant a 2-year renewal at the licensee's request only if specified conditions are met in the preceding 24 months.
- **210 ILCS 9/70**: Service requirements. Defines medication reminders, supervision of self-administered medication, and medication administration, and who may perform each (including certified medication aides under RN supervision and delegation, with stated exclusions). Services may be provided directly or arranged with resident consent.
- **210 ILCS 9/135**: Civil penalties. IDPH may assess up to $5,000 per violation (each day a separate violation) and up to $3,000 per day for caring for a resident who exceeds the care needs defined in the Act. Repeated technical infractions within a calendar year may become a Type 3 violation. IDPH may hold hearings on appeals.
- **210 ILCS 9/150**: Alzheimer and dementia programs. Limits on admission and retention, validated dementia-specific assessment standards, physician signature on annual and change-of-condition assessments, and requirements for establishments offering a special dementia program (disclosure, designated representative, wandering and evacuation safety policies, family communication, activities, staffing, dementia training, and emergency procedures).
- **Public Act 104-0589 (HB 3392)**: Amends 210 ILCS 9/15, 35, 70, 135 and 150. The ILGA page shows an effective date of 7/24/2026 while Section 99 states it is effective on becoming law, so verify the operative date.
- **225 ILCS 46**: Health Care Worker Background Check Act. Applies to employees with or who may have resident contact. Fingerprints are collected electronically and sent to the Illinois State Police within 10 working days.

### B. Administrative Rules

- **77 Ill. Adm. Code 295**: Assisted Living and Shared Housing Establishment Code (IDPH). Organized as Subpart A General Provisions (295.1-295.1110); B Policies (295.2000-295.2080); C Personnel (295.3000-295.3050); D Resident Care and Services (295.4000-295.4060); E Medications (295.5000); F Resident Rights (295.6000-295.6030); G Resident and Establishment Records (295.7000-295.7010); H Food Service (295.8000); I Physical Plant and Environmental Requirements (295.9000-295.9040). Amendments are noted through 7/29/2024.
- **77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.500**: Application for License. Nonrefundable fee ($2,000 + $20 per unit for assisted living; $1,000 for shared housing), standard vs. floating licensure, liability insurance documentation, and financial capacity.
- **77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.600**: Initial license issuance. IDPH issues a regular license within 120 days of a complete application, subject to fees paid, substantial compliance, and Background Check Act compliance.
- **77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2000**: Residency Requirements. An establishment may not accept or retain a resident when it lacks appropriate staff in numbers and skill or cannot provide or secure required services. Read the full text for the complete list of conditions.
- **77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030**: Establishment Contracts. Required title, 12-point minimum type, and the required contract elements, including license status, base rate and services, extra services and fees, complaint process with notice of the Department on Aging Senior Helpline and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, the Medicaid statement, admission and termination criteria, a risk management statement, the Section 95 rights list, and an IDPH statement on the annual on-site review process. Also covers fee/deposit/refund terms, 30 days' written notice of fee changes (with the stated exception), emergency/relative notification policy, copies to the resident or representative, and written, signed changes.
- **77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000**: Personnel Requirements, Qualifications and Training. Sufficient qualified staff for 24-hour needs; at least one direct care staff person on duty at all times with adult CPR training and current certification; direct care staff 16+ at hire; job descriptions; employee file contents; record retention for employment plus at least 12 months; awake-staff requirements; Nurse Aide Registry check before hire; and license verification for licensed staff. Check this against the current JCAR text.
- **89 Ill. Adm. Code 146**: Supportive Living Program (HFS). Medicaid rules that apply **only** if the facility is separately approved and certified by HFS. They do not apply to an IDPH-licensed, private-pay-only establishment.

### C. Regulators and Contact Information

Contact details are listed only where they were provided. Where none is shown, use the website listed and confirm current phone and email there. **[AGENCY NAME]** should enter verified contacts in the bracketed fields.

Email: HFS.SLF@illinois.gov. Web: https://hfs.illinois.gov/medicalclients/hcbs/slf.html |

The contract rule (77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030) also requires notice of the **Department on Aging Senior Helpline** and the **Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program**. Insert their current contact information in resident contracts and posted notices: **[verify and insert]**.

### D. Customization, Adoption, Currency, and Training

This framework is a starting point and does not replace legal review. **[AGENCY NAME]** must customize every placeholder, have the **[GOVERNING BODY]** formally adopt the manual, keep it current as statutes, rules, and agency guidance change, and train all staff on it with documented records.

citations.title: Assessment and service plan requirements
citations.requirement: Before admission, a comprehensive assessment of physical, cognitive and psychosocial condition must be completed by a physician, physician assistant or APRN. It must be repeated at least annually and on a significant change in condition, including a diagnosis of Alzheimer's or a related dementia. IDPH may set more frequent skin-integrity and nutrition assessments by rule. A written service plan is mutually agreed by provider, resident and representative and reviewed at least annually or when needs change. On request the resident or representative gets a copy of the latest assessment, any supplemental establishment assessment, and the service plan. Text as amended by P.A. 104-0589.

citations.title: Issuance of license
citations.requirement: A full-time director must be 21+ with a high school diploma or equivalent plus qualifying experience (35(a)(2)). Staff must be sufficient in number and skill for 24-hour scheduled and unscheduled needs and must take ongoing training (35(a)(3)). All employees subject to the Health Care Worker Background Check Act must meet it (35(a)(4)). Applicant must file the Alzheimer's/dementia special care disclosure document (35(a)(7)). As a condition of licensure the director must complete at least 20 hours of training every 2 years. Licenses last one year, state the physical location, issue and expiration dates, and are not transferable.

citations.title: Service requirements
citations.requirement: Defines medication reminders, supervision of self-administered medication and medication administration. Medication administration is by a licensed health care professional employed by the establishment. A certified medication aide may administer under RN supervision and delegation per Nurse Practice Act 50-75, except Schedule II controlled substances and any subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal or IV medication. Supervision of self-administered medication is under a licensed health care professional, or under RN delegation for a certified medication aide. IDPH sets procedures by rule. Services may be provided directly or by others arranged with resident consent.

citations.title: Civil penalties
citations.requirement: IDPH may assess a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation, with each day a separate violation. A penalty of up to $3,000 (also per day) may be assessed for caring for a resident who exceeds the care needs defined in the Act. Repeated technical infractions within a calendar year may become a Type 3 violation. IDPH may hold hearings on appeals.

citations.title: Alzheimer and dementia programs
citations.requirement: No admission or retention if the establishment cannot provide or secure appropriate care or lacks appropriately skilled staff. Residency is barred if the resident's condition has so deteriorated that residency is detrimental to the resident or others, or if the resident is dangerous and the danger cannot be eliminated. IDPH rule must identify a validated dementia-specific assessment standard with inter-rater reliability. That assessment is approved by the physician, or a PA/APRN with geriatric dementia experience. It is done before acceptance, annually, and on a change in condition. Annual and change-of-condition assessments must be signed by a physician. Establishments offering a special dementia program must disclose to IDPH and residents, ensure a designated representative, adopt wandering and evacuation safety policies, coordinate communications with family, provide cognitive stimulation and activities, staff appropriately, provide director and direct care staff dementia training, and have emergency procedures and staffing patterns. Pre-admission assessment tools must be validated for dementia-related cognitive impairment (150(g)).

Awake staff are required for residents who cannot self-move to safety (j). Shared housing needs at least one staff member on site at all times (k). Assisted living needs at least one staff member awake, on duty and on site 24 hours (l). Nurse Aide Registry check before hire, with no hiring of anyone with a finding of abuse, neglect or misappropriation (m). Licensed-staff license verification (n). Cornell shows this section's history as last amended in 2004, so check it against the current JCAR text.

policies.title: Organization, Governing Body and Director/Manager Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: Assisted living establishment and shared housing establishment; governing body, director/manager, designated backup, and all supervisory staff
policies.purpose: To define how [AGENCY NAME] is organized and governed, who is accountable for the establishment's operation, and the qualifications, training and coverage requirements for the full-time director/manager, so that the establishment is always under qualified management and meets the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act and 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is governed by a governing body that holds ultimate legal responsibility for the establishment. The governing body appoints a full-time director (called the "manager" in the IDPH rules) who is accountable for daily operations, resident care and services, staffing, and compliance with the Act and Part 295. The two terms are used interchangeably in this manual. The director/manager must be at least 21 years old, hold a high school diploma or equivalent, and meet the Act's experience or education requirement. The director/manager must complete at least 20 hours of training every 2 years as a condition of licensure. A qualified backup is named in writing at all times so the full-time director requirement is never left unmet.

definitions.definition: The full-time individual appointed by the governing body to be responsible for the day-to-day operation of the establishment. The Act uses "director"; the IDPH rules use "manager."
The owner, board, members or managers of [AGENCY NAME] who hold legal authority and ultimate responsibility for the establishment.

Management or progressive-responsibility experience in health care, housing with services, adult day care or similar services to the elderly, as recognized by the Act. The Act also permits a hospitality-experience-plus-training route, or a college degree in health administration or an approved program completed within 6 months of hire.
A qualified person named in writing by the governing body to act with the director/manager's authority during absences, so that the establishment is never without a responsible manager.

procedures: The governing body adopts a written organizational chart and a written statement of the director/manager's authority and duties, and reviews both at least annually.
The governing body records the legal name of the licensee, the owners or members, and the establishment's physical address in the governing body minutes and in this manual ([AGENCY NAME], [ADDRESS]).

Before offering the director/manager position, the governing body verifies in writing that the candidate is at least 21 years old, holds a high school diploma or equivalent (copy of diploma or transcript), and meets the Act's experience or education route. Verification includes prior-employer references.

The governing body documents which qualification route the director/manager meets (2 years of qualifying experience; hospitality experience plus training; or a college degree in health administration or an approved program completed within 6 months of hire) and keeps the supporting evidence in the personnel file.
The director/manager completes the Health Care Worker Background Check Act process before starting work and is checked against the employee registries (see STF-02).
The director/manager is employed full time. [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] is the current director/manager and may be reached at [PHONE].

The governing body names at least one qualified backup in writing. The backup meets the same age, education and experience requirements as the director/manager, or the governing body documents how the backup is qualified. The backup list is posted for staff and updated within 5 working days of any change.
When the director/manager is absent, the designated backup is on site or immediately reachable by phone. The staff schedule identifies who is the person in charge on every shift.

The director/manager completes at least 20 hours of training in each 2-year period. Topics are relevant to assisted living management, resident care, regulation, and the Act's requirements. The director/manager keeps certificates, dates and hours in a training log kept in the personnel file, and the governing body reviews the log every 6 months.

If the director/manager position becomes vacant, the governing body appoints a qualified interim director/manager immediately so that full-time management is not interrupted, and begins recruitment within 5 working days.

[AGENCY NAME] notifies IDPH in writing of a change in director/manager. As an internal standard, notice is sent within 10 working days of the change or sooner if the current rule text requires it. The governing body confirms the exact deadline against the current Part 295 text at each annual policy review.

[AGENCY NAME] will not assign one manager to more than one establishment, including any arrangement allowed for shared housing, until the governing body has confirmed the conditions in the current Part 295 text and recorded the decision in the minutes.

The director/manager ensures the establishment meets the mandatory staffing rules: for assisted living, at least one staff member awake, on duty and on site 24 hours a day and at least one CPR-certified direct care staff member on duty at all times; for shared housing, at least one staff member on site at all times (see STF-01).

The director/manager reports to the governing body at least quarterly on census, staffing, incidents, grievances, survey activity, training status and quality improvement results, and the governing body records its review and any directions in minutes.
The governing body evaluates the director/manager's performance at least annually against the duties in this policy and documents the evaluation.

responsibilities.duty: Appoints and evaluates the director/manager, names the backup, confirms qualifications, ensures the establishment is licensed and adequately resourced, and reviews quarterly reports.
Runs daily operations, enforces policies, maintains staffing and training compliance, completes required training hours, and reports to the governing body.
Assumes director/manager authority during absences and documents decisions and events during the coverage period.
Maintains qualification evidence, training logs and IDPH change notices in the personnel and governance files.

documentation: Organizational chart and written director/manager duty statement
Director/manager qualification file (diploma or equivalent, experience verification, qualification route)
Director/manager training log and certificates (20 hours every 2 years)
Written designation of backup and coverage schedules
Governing body minutes and quarterly reports
Copies of IDPH notices of director/manager changes
Annual director/manager evaluation

policies.title: Licensure, Posting and Regulatory Compliance
policies.applies_to: Assisted living establishment and shared housing establishment; governing body, director/manager and business office
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] holds a current IDPH license before operating, keeps it in good standing, renews it on time, displays it, and follows the Act and Part 295, avoiding civil penalties and loss of licensure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not establish, operate, maintain or offer an assisted living or shared housing establishment without a license issued by the Illinois Department of Public Health. The license is valid for one year, states the physical location, and is issued only for the premises and persons named. It cannot be transferred or assigned. The director/manager tracks renewal dates, civil penalty exposure, and changes in law, including Public Act 104-0589, and the governing body holds ultimate accountability for compliance.

definitions.definition: The written authorization issued by IDPH that permits [AGENCY NAME] to operate an assisted living or shared housing establishment at the stated physical location for one year.
The licensure basis stated in the application. [AGENCY NAME] states which basis it is applying under, and that basis governs how the establishment's units are licensed.
IDPH classifications of violations by seriousness. Violation history affects eligibility for a 2-year renewal and civil penalty exposure.
A monetary penalty IDPH may assess for violations of the Act or rules. It may be up to $5,000 per violation with each day a separate violation.

procedures: Before any resident is admitted, the director/manager confirms that a current IDPH license is in hand. No marketing, contracting, admission or occupancy for care purposes takes place before licensure.

For the initial application, the governing body submits the completed application and the nonrefundable fee: $2,000 plus $20 per unit for assisted living, or $1,000 for shared housing. The application states standard or floating licensure and includes liability insurance documentation and evidence of financial capacity. The business office keeps a copy of the application, proof of payment and the submission date.
The Alzheimer's/dementia special care disclosure document is filed with the application as the Act requires (see HCS-05).

The director/manager confirms all covered employees have met the Health Care Worker Background Check Act before IDPH approval, as approval requires compliance. IDPH issues a regular license within 120 days of a complete application. The director/manager tracks that date and responds to IDPH requests for information within the deadline stated in the request.
On receipt, the director/manager checks the license for the correct legal name, physical location, issue date and expiration date. Any error is reported to IDPH in writing within 5 working days.

[AGENCY NAME] posts the license in a conspicuous place that residents and visitors can see, as agency practice, together with other postings required by Part 295. The director/manager reviews posting requirements at each annual policy review.
The business office enters the license expiration date in the compliance calendar and sets reminders at 180, 150 and 120 days before expiration.
The renewal application and fee are filed between 120 and 150 days before expiration. The director/manager signs the application and keeps proof of timely filing.

A 2-year renewal is discretionary with IDPH and is requested only if, in the preceding 24 months, there was no Type 1 or Type 2 violation, no inspection with 10 or more Type 3 violations, and no admission or retention of a resident in violation of Section 75 of the Act. The director/manager checks this eligibility before requesting it and records the result.

The license is not transferred or assigned. Before any change of ownership, change of physical location, or other change that affects the license, the governing body contacts IDPH in writing to learn what new licensing is required, and does not proceed with the change until the licensing path is confirmed.

The director/manager makes sure the establishment does not admit or retain a resident who exceeds the care needs defined in the Act (see ADM-04), because IDPH may assess a penalty of up to $3,000 per day for caring for such a resident.

On receipt of any IDPH statement of violations or notice of civil penalty, the director/manager notifies the governing body within 1 working day, calendars all response and appeal deadlines, prepares a written plan of correction, and keeps the response on file. IDPH may hold hearings on appeals.

The director/manager monitors technical infractions. Repeated technical infractions in a calendar year may become a Type 3 violation, so the director/manager tracks repeat findings and corrects root causes (see GOV-04).

The director/manager monitors the Illinois Register, the ILGA and JCAR websites, and IDPH communications for changes in the Act and Part 295. Public Act 104-0589 amends Sections 15, 35, 70, 135 and 150 of the Act, and its effective date is shown as July 24, 2026. The director/manager confirms that date against the Public Act text and updates policies before it takes effect (see GOV-03).
The governing body reviews licensure status, renewal calendar, violation history and regulatory changes at least quarterly and records the review in minutes.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the establishment is licensed before operating, funds the license fees, signs the application, and decides on changes in ownership or location.
Manages the application, renewal calendar, posting, IDPH correspondence and regulatory tracking, and ensures compliance.
Maintains the compliance calendar, proof of fee payment and copies of all filings.

documentation: License application, fee receipt and submission proof
Current license and prior licenses
Renewal calendar and renewal filing proof
Eligibility check for 2-year renewal
IDPH notices, statements of violation, plans of correction and appeal records
Regulatory change log (including Public Act 104-0589)
Quarterly governing body review minutes

policies.title: Policy Review and Document Control
policies.applies_to: All policies and procedures of [AGENCY NAME]; director/manager and governing body
policies.purpose: To keep every policy current, consistent with the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act and 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295, controlled by version, and accessible to staff and surveyors.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reviews every policy at least annually and whenever a statute or rule changes. The director/manager keeps a version log, and each policy lists the Part 295 and Act citations on which it is based. Public Act 104-0589, shown as effective July 24, 2026, is an immediate review trigger.

definitions.definition: The process of approving, numbering, dating, distributing, revising and retiring policies so that only the current version is in use.
An event that requires review outside the annual cycle, such as a new law, a rule amendment, an IDPH finding, or an internal incident showing a policy gap.
A record listing each policy's ID, version number, effective date, reviewer, summary of changes and approver.

procedures: The director/manager keeps a master index of all policies by ID and title, with the current version number and effective date for each.
Each policy shows its ID, title, version, effective date, last review date, approver and the Act and Part 295 citations on which it relies.
Each policy is reviewed at least once every 12 months. The director/manager assigns each review to a named reviewer and sets due dates in the compliance calendar.

Before each annual review, the director/manager re-checks the ILGA and JCAR websites for amendments to Part 295 made after the most recent amendments noted in published sources (amendments through July 29, 2024) and records the date and result of that check.

Public Act 104-0589 is an immediate trigger. Within 30 days of the review start, and in any event before the date it takes effect, the director/manager reviews every affected policy, including those on admission assessment, director training, medications, dementia care and penalties, confirms the effective date against the Public Act text, and revises as needed.

Other triggers include a new or amended statute or rule, IDPH guidance, a statement of violations, a serious incident, a change in services offered, and a change in ownership or management. Triggered reviews begin within 10 working days.

The reviewer compares the policy against the current statute and rule text, records proposed changes, and sends them to the director/manager for approval and to the governing body for adoption when the change is substantive.
Approved revisions receive a new version number and effective date. The version log is updated the same day.
The director/manager distributes revised policies to affected staff within 5 working days of the effective date, trains staff on substantive changes, and collects signed acknowledgements.
Superseded versions are marked "superseded," removed from working binders and electronic folders, and archived for at least 5 years, or longer if required by a retention rule.
A current copy of the manual is kept on site and available to all staff at all times and to IDPH surveyors on request.
The governing body reviews the version log and compliance calendar at least annually to confirm that no policy is overdue.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the manual and substantive revisions and verifies annual review completion.
Owns document control, assigns reviewers, monitors regulatory changes, trains staff and maintains the version log.
Compare policies against current law, propose revisions and document the review.
Use only current policies and sign acknowledgements of revised policies.

documentation: Master policy index and version log
Annual review records and regulatory check records
Public Act 104-0589 review file
Staff acknowledgement and training sign-in sheets
Archive of superseded policies
Governing body adoption minutes

policies.title: Quality Improvement Program and Risk Management
policies.applies_to: Assisted living establishment and shared housing establishment; governing body, director/manager, nursing and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To maintain a quality improvement program and risk management process that identifies problems, reduces harm to residents, and drives correction, consistent with IDPH requirements and the establishment contract, which must state that a risk management process is maintained.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written quality improvement (QI) program and a risk management process. The establishment contract states that the establishment maintains a risk management process. Data from incidents, grievances, falls, medication errors and infection surveillance are reviewed regularly, and corrective actions are tracked to completion. The director/manager confirms the specific elements, meeting frequency and documentation required by the current IDPH quality improvement rule at each annual policy review, and this policy is revised if the rule requires more than is stated here.

definitions.definition: A planned, ongoing process of collecting and analyzing data about resident care and operations and acting on findings to improve outcomes.
The process by which the establishment identifies, evaluates and reduces risks to residents, staff and visitors, and informs residents of this process through the establishment contract.
A written plan listing the problem, root cause, actions, responsible person, due date and the measure used to verify success.

procedures: The governing body adopts a written QI plan each year that names the QI lead (the director/manager unless otherwise assigned), the data sources and the review schedule.

The QI committee includes the director/manager, the nurse or nursing designee, and a direct care, dietary or activity staff member. The governing body may add outside members, such as a consulting pharmacist or the medical director.
The QI committee meets at least quarterly as an internal standard. The director/manager records attendees, topics, decisions and assignments in minutes at each meeting.

The director/manager compiles and presents the following data at each meeting: incidents and accidents (SAF-02), grievances and complaints (RR-02), falls (HCS-06), medication errors (HCS-01, HCS-02), infection surveillance (SAF-07), skin integrity events (HCS-07), elopement events (SAF-03), and hospital transfers (HCS-04).
The committee looks for trends by resident, unit, shift, staff, time of day and cause, and flags repeat events for root cause analysis.
For each identified problem, the committee writes a corrective action plan with an owner and due date. The director/manager tracks all plans on one log until closed.
The director/manager verifies completion of each corrective action and re-checks the relevant measure at the next meeting. Plans that did not work are revised.

Risk management steps: the director/manager identifies risks at least annually through environmental rounds, resident assessments, negotiated risk agreements (ADM-06) and staff input, and records the risks and controls.
The risk management process is described in the establishment contract signed by each resident or representative (RR-04). The director/manager checks that the statement is in every contract.
Resident and family input, including satisfaction surveys and Resident Council feedback where applicable, is reviewed each quarter and counted in the QI data.
QI findings that require staff education are turned into in-service training within 30 days (STF-03).

QI records are confidential and kept separately from resident records. They are available to IDPH surveyors as requested, and the director/manager reports QI results to the governing body at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts the QI plan, reviews QI reports and provides resources for corrective action.
Leads the QI program, compiles data, chairs meetings, assigns and verifies corrective actions.
Provides clinical data and analysis on falls, medications, skin integrity, infections and changes of condition.
Report incidents, near misses and concerns promptly and take part in corrective actions.

documentation: Annual QI plan
QI meeting agendas, sign-in sheets and minutes
Data summaries and trend reports
Corrective action plan log and closure verification
Risk assessment record
Governing body QI reports

policies.title: Compliance, Fraud and Billing Integrity
policies.applies_to: Assisted living establishment and shared housing establishment; governing body, director/manager, business office and any staff involved in billing, contracts or resident funds
policies.purpose: To ensure that all charges are accurate, consistent with the establishment contract and honestly billed, that residents are told accurately about payment sources, and that any future Supportive Living Program participation is handled under the separate HFS rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a private-pay establishment licensed by IDPH. Each establishment contract states that Medicaid (Article V or VI of the Illinois Public Aid Code) does not pay for services in the establishment. Billing must match the contract's base rate, additional-service fee schedule and billing procedures. [AGENCY NAME] does not participate in the HFS Supportive Living Program. If the governing body separately seeks and obtains HFS approval and certification, a Supportive Living Program addendum under 89 Ill. Adm. Code 146 will be adopted before any Medicaid resident is served; until then, that Part does not apply. Medicare- or Medicaid-certification-based compliance programs do not apply to the private-pay licensure program.

definitions.definition: The regular charge stated in the establishment contract for housing and the services included in the base rate.
The list of services not included in the base rate and their charges, stated in the contract and given to residents.

The Medicaid program operated by HFS under 89 Ill. Adm. Code 146. It applies only to facilities separately approved and certified by HFS, and does not apply to a private-pay IDPH-licensed establishment.
Knowingly charging for services not provided, charging more than the contract allows, or falsifying records to support a charge.

procedures: Every establishment contract includes the statement that Medicaid is not available for services in the establishment, the base rate and services, the extra services and fee schedule, and the billing procedures. The director/manager checks each contract for these items before signature (RR-04).
Before admission, staff explain the base rate, extra-service charges, deposits and refund terms to the resident or representative, and give a copy of the signed contract.
Staff do not tell residents or families that Medicaid will pay or may pay for care in the establishment, and do not suggest that [AGENCY NAME] participates in the Supportive Living Program.

The business office prepares each resident's monthly invoice only from the contract's base rate and the fee schedule, and only for services that the service plan and service records show were actually provided (ADM-03).
Additional-service charges require a service record showing date, service, staff name and time or units. The director/manager or nurse signs off on additional-service charges before they are billed.

Fee changes are made only in writing, with at least 30 days' written notice to the resident or representative. Notice is not required where a charge changes because the resident's service needs changed under the service plan. The business office keeps a copy of each notice and proof of delivery.
Deposits, refunds and resident funds are handled under RR-04 and RR-05, and refunds are issued within the time stated in the contract.

The director/manager samples at least 10 percent of resident invoices (or at least 5, whichever is greater) each quarter and compares them with the contract and service records. Errors are corrected, residents are credited or refunded within 30 days of discovery, and the cause is recorded.

Staff who find or suspect billing errors, false records or improper charges report them to the director/manager immediately. Reports may be made to the governing body if the concern involves the director/manager. No staff member will be retaliated against for a report made in good faith.
Billing and records responsibilities are separated, so that no single person both authorizes a charge and receives payment without review by a second person.

The governing body reviews billing audit results and any reports of billing concerns at least quarterly. Findings of intentional misbilling result in discipline up to termination and, where required, a report to the appropriate authority.

Civil penalties under the Act may be assessed for violations, and each day may be a separate violation. The director/manager treats violations of contract and disclosure requirements as compliance risks and corrects them promptly (GOV-02).

If the governing body decides to seek HFS Supportive Living certification, it first obtains HFS approval and certification, adopts an SLP addendum covering 89 Ill. Adm. Code 146 requirements (including quarterly quality-metric reporting through the HFS portal and the federal home and community-based settings requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c)), updates the contract and this manual (GOV-03), and trains staff before serving any Medicaid participant.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the base rate and fee schedule, reviews billing audits, and decides whether to seek HFS certification.
Ensures contracts, charges and invoices are accurate and consistent, conducts quarterly audits and investigates reports.
Prepare invoices from the contract and service records, keep notices and proof of delivery, and process credits and refunds.
Record services accurately, report billing concerns and make no statements about Medicaid payment.

documentation: Signed establishment contracts with Medicaid statement, rates and fee schedule
Resident invoices and service records supporting additional charges
30-day fee change notices and proof of delivery
Quarterly billing audit worksheets and corrective actions
Credit and refund records
Reports of billing concerns and investigation records
SLP addendum and HFS certification documents (only if applicable)

policies.title: Annual IDPH On-Site Review and Survey Readiness
policies.applies_to: Assisted living establishment and shared housing establishment; governing body, director/manager and all staff
policies.purpose: To keep [AGENCY NAME] ready for IDPH on-site reviews at all times, to ensure each resident is told about the review process, and to manage survey results so that violation history does not put licensure or 2-year renewal eligibility at risk.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is subject to an annual IDPH on-site review. Each establishment contract must include an IDPH statement describing the annual on-site review process and which resident-file documents the reviewer examines. Resident files, contracts, assessments, service plans, personnel files, training records and staff schedules are kept survey-ready at all times. One staff member is named as IDPH liaison. Type 1, Type 2 and Type 3 violation history affects eligibility for a 2-year license renewal.

definitions.definition: The on-site review of the establishment performed by IDPH under the Act, which includes examination of resident files and other records and observation of care and the environment.
The staff member named by the director/manager to coordinate with surveyors, track correspondence and deadlines, and keep the survey log.
A written response to IDPH survey findings that states how and when each deficiency will be corrected.
The state of having all required records complete, accurate and promptly retrievable, and all staff able to explain their duties.

procedures: The director/manager confirms that each establishment contract includes the IDPH statement on the annual on-site review process, including the resident-file documents the reviewer examines, and gives it to residents and representatives with the signed contract (RR-04).
The director/manager names the IDPH liaison in writing. The liaison is [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] unless another named person is designated, and a backup liaison is also named.
The liaison keeps a survey log recording each IDPH contact: date, IDPH staff, subject, requests, response due date, and the date the response was sent.

The director/manager keeps a survey-readiness binder or electronic folder with the current license, the policy manual, the staff roster and schedules, the resident census and floor plan, emergency and evacuation plans, and drill records.

Resident files are audited every quarter for completeness, including the signed contract, assessments, service plans, physician orders, medication records, and notices. The director/manager records missing items, assigns correction, and verifies it within 14 days.

Personnel files are audited every quarter for completeness: background check and registry results, qualifications, training records, health and TB screening and acknowledgements (STF-02 through STF-05).

The director/manager carries out an internal mock review at least twice a year using the Act and Part 295 as the checklist. Results are written up, deficiencies are assigned and corrected, and findings are reported to the governing body.

Because surveys are unannounced, all staff are told how to handle a surveyor's arrival: greet and verify identification, notify the director/manager or person in charge immediately, and cooperate. Staff do not hide or alter records.

On arrival of surveyors, the person in charge notifies the liaison, who escorts the surveyors, provides records on request, takes notes of questions and requests, and keeps a copy list of documents provided.
The director/manager makes staff and residents available for interviews as requested, and does not discourage or retaliate against any resident or staff member who speaks to a surveyor.
At the exit conference, the director/manager or liaison attends, notes each finding, and asks for clarification of the cited requirement. The notes are filed in the survey log.

On receipt of the written statement of violations, the director/manager reviews it within 1 working day, notifies the governing body, and calendars the plan-of-correction due date and any appeal deadline stated by IDPH.
The plan of correction states the cause, the action, the responsible person, the completion date and how correction will be monitored. It is submitted by the IDPH deadline and a copy is kept.
Corrections are carried out and verified, and evidence of correction (such as revised policies, training sign-ins, audits and photographs) is filed with the survey record.

The director/manager reviews each survey's results against the 2-year renewal eligibility criteria: no Type 1 or Type 2 violation, no inspection with 10 or more Type 3 violations, and no admission or retention in violation of Section 75 of the Act in the preceding 24 months. The result is recorded and considered at renewal planning (GOV-02).
Survey findings are entered into the quality improvement program, and repeat findings receive a root cause analysis (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Reviews survey results and mock review reports, provides resources for correction and approves plans of correction.
Ensures readiness, leads mock reviews, prepares plans of correction and verifies corrections.
Coordinates with IDPH, keeps the survey log and tracks deadlines.
Keep records complete and accurate, cooperate with surveyors and report concerns.

documentation: Contract statement on the IDPH annual on-site review process
Written designation of IDPH liaison and backup
Survey log and correspondence file
Quarterly resident file and personnel file audit results
Mock review reports and corrective actions
IDPH statements of violations, plans of correction, evidence of correction
Renewal eligibility review record

policies.title: Resident Rights and Responsibilities
policies.applies_to: All residents, residents' representatives, and all staff of [AGENCY NAME], whether licensed as an assisted living establishment or a shared housing establishment
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident knows, receives, and can exercise the rights guaranteed by the Illinois Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act, and understands the responsibilities that come with residency at [AGENCY NAME].
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] honors every right listed in Section 95 of the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act. Signing the establishment contract does not waive or forfeit any of those rights. The complete Section 95 rights list is printed in each resident's contract, posted in a public area, and explained to residents and representatives in a language and format they understand. Residents also have the responsibilities stated in the contract. Those responsibilities are never used to restrict a right. Staff will not retaliate against any resident for exercising a right, filing a complaint, or contacting an outside agency.

definitions.definition: The list of resident rights in Section 95 of the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act (210 ILCS 9), which must be listed in the establishment contract.
A person designated by the resident, or authorized by law, to act on the resident's behalf. See RR-09.
Any adverse action, threat, or change in treatment taken because a resident or another person exercised a right or raised a concern.

procedures: The Administrator keeps the full text of the Section 95 rights, copied exactly from the current Act and Department rules, as Attachment A to this policy. The Administrator checks it against the published text at each annual policy review (GOV-03) and whenever the Act is amended.
The Administrator posts Attachment A in a conspicuous public area that residents and visitors can reach, at the same location as the license (GOV-02). It is posted in large, legible print.

Before move-in, the Administrator or designee gives the resident and any representative a copy of the contract, which includes the Section 95 rights list, the statement that contracting does not forfeit those rights, and the resident responsibilities (RR-04).

The designee reviews the rights and responsibilities aloud with the resident and representative in plain language, in the resident's preferred language, using an interpreter or auxiliary aids where needed (RR-08). The designee allows time for questions and for the resident to consult family, counsel, or the Ombudsman before signing.
The resident or representative signs an acknowledgment that the rights and responsibilities were given and explained. The signed acknowledgment is filed in the resident record (REC-01).

The Administrator trains every new employee on resident rights during orientation, before the employee provides care without supervision, and again at least annually (STF-03). Attendance is documented.

Staff protect rights in daily care. Staff knock and wait before entering private rooms. They protect privacy during personal care and keep resident information confidential (RR-07). They support residents in making their own choices about daily routines, visitors, and the use of personal belongings.

The Administrator makes sure no house rule, schedule, or staff instruction restricts a right. Any proposed limit on a right is reviewed by the Administrator, tied to a documented safety reason, and addressed through the service plan or a negotiated risk agreement (ADM-03, ADM-06).

The Administrator reviews resident responsibilities at least yearly to confirm they match the contract. Where a resident does not meet a responsibility, staff first try to understand why and offer help. Staff do not respond by limiting a right.

Any staff member who sees or hears of a possible rights violation reports it to the Administrator the same shift. Possible abuse, neglect, or exploitation is handled under SAF-01 immediately, and other concerns are handled under RR-02.
The Administrator investigates each reported rights concern, takes corrective action, informs the resident or representative of the outcome, and logs the concern for QI review (GOV-04).

The Administrator reminds residents at least yearly, through a resident meeting or written notice, of their rights, of how to file a complaint, and that the Ombudsman and IDPH are available to them (RR-02, RR-03).
The Administrator reviews rights-related complaints and observations quarterly in the QI program and takes corrective action where patterns appear.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains and posts the rights list, makes sure contracts and acknowledgments are complete, investigates rights concerns, and ensures no retaliation.
Explains rights and responsibilities to each resident and representative before signing, and files the signed acknowledgment.
Complete rights training, honor resident rights in daily care, and report suspected violations immediately.
Reviews rights-related QI findings and supports corrective action.

documentation: Attachment A: current Section 95 rights list, with date of last verification
Signed contract and signed rights and responsibilities acknowledgment in the resident record
Staff orientation and annual training sign-in sheets
Rights concern log and investigation notes
Record of the posting date and location

policies.title: Grievances and Complaints
policies.applies_to: All residents, residents' representatives, family members, and staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give residents and representatives a clear, safe, and prompt way to raise complaints, to make sure each complaint is answered, and to use complaint data to improve care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has a written complaint resolution process, described in each establishment contract. Residents and representatives may complain orally or in writing, to any staff member, at any time, without fear of retaliation. The contract and the postings also give notice of the Illinois Department on Aging Senior Helpline and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program, and of how to contact IDPH. Using the internal process is never required before contacting an outside agency. Every complaint is logged, answered within the timeframes below, and reviewed in the QI program.

definitions.definition: Any concern or dissatisfaction a resident, representative, or family member expresses about care, services, staff, other residents, fees, or the environment.
The Illinois Department on Aging telephone line listed in the contract and posted for residents. Number: [SENIOR HELPLINE NUMBER].
The program that advocates for residents of long-term care settings and helps resolve complaints. Regional contact: [REGIONAL OMBUDSMAN NAME AND PHONE].

procedures: The Administrator designates a Grievance Coordinator ([GRIEVANCE COORDINATOR NAME]). The Administrator is the coordinator unless another person is named in writing.
At move-in, the admissions designee gives the resident and representative the complaint process in writing. It is part of the contract. The designee explains it verbally and confirms understanding.

The Administrator posts the complaint process with these contact numbers in a public area: the Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR PHONE]; IDPH complaint line, [IDPH COMPLAINT LINE]; Department on Aging Senior Helpline, [SENIOR HELPLINE NUMBER]; and the regional Ombudsman, [REGIONAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE]. The Administrator verifies all numbers against current IDPH and Department on Aging sources at least every six months and whenever a number changes.

Any staff member who receives a complaint listens, treats it respectfully, and records it on the Grievance Form the same shift. Staff help residents who cannot write to complete the form. Anonymous complaints are accepted and reviewed.

The staff member gives the form to the Grievance Coordinator by the end of the next business day. Any complaint that suggests abuse, neglect, exploitation, or immediate danger is reported to the Administrator at once and handled under SAF-01 and SAF-02, with no delay for the grievance process.

The Grievance Coordinator enters the complaint in the Grievance Log with the date received, complainant, nature of complaint, and staff involved. The Coordinator acknowledges the complaint to the complainant within two business days.

The Coordinator investigates promptly. This includes interviewing the complainant, involved staff, and any witnesses, and reviewing the resident record and any relevant incident reports. Staff who are the subject of the complaint do not investigate it.

The Coordinator gives the complainant a written resolution that describes the findings and any action taken. The goal is within 10 business days of receipt. If more time is needed, the Coordinator tells the complainant why and gives a new date.

If the complainant is not satisfied, the Coordinator explains the right to appeal to the Administrator or the governing body and reminds the complainant of the Senior Helpline, the Ombudsman, and IDPH.
The Administrator prohibits retaliation. Any report of retaliation is investigated as a separate complaint and may lead to discipline under STF-06.

If IDPH, the Ombudsman, or another agency contacts the establishment about a complaint, the Administrator cooperates fully and promptly provides records requested and permitted by law, and documents the contact.

The Administrator keeps the Grievance Log and summarizes complaints by type, location, and outcome for the quarterly QI meeting (GOV-04). Corrective actions are assigned to a named person with a due date.
At least yearly, the Administrator asks residents and representatives, for example at a resident meeting, whether they know how to complain and whether they feel safe doing so. Results are recorded.

responsibilities.duty: Oversees the process, ensures no retaliation, posts verified contact numbers, and presents data to QI.
Logs, investigates, acknowledges, resolves, and communicates the outcome for each complaint.
Accept complaints courteously, record them on the form the same shift, and escalate safety concerns immediately.
Reviews complaint trends quarterly and tracks corrective actions.

documentation: Grievance Form for each complaint
Grievance Log
Written acknowledgment and resolution letters
Investigation notes and corrective action records
Record of the six-month contact-number verification
QI meeting minutes reflecting complaint review

policies.title: Ombudsman Access
policies.applies_to: All residents, residents' representatives, and all staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents know the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program is available to help resolve complaints, and that Ombudsman representatives can reach and speak privately with residents.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] tells every resident, in the establishment contract and through postings, that the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program is available to help resolve complaints. Ombudsman representatives may visit residents and speak with them privately, and staff will not obstruct, discourage, or retaliate against any resident for contacting the Ombudsman. Resident records are released to the Ombudsman only as permitted by law and with the resident's consent or as otherwise legally authorized.

definitions.definition: A staff member or certified volunteer of the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program who presents identification.
A conversation between a resident and an Ombudsman representative that staff cannot hear or interrupt.

procedures: The Administrator posts the regional Ombudsman name, address, and telephone number, plus the Department on Aging Senior Helpline, in a public area, and includes them in the resident handbook. The Administrator verifies the information with the Illinois Department on Aging at least every six months and records the check.

At move-in, the admissions designee points out the Ombudsman notice in the contract, explains in plain language that the Ombudsman is independent of the establishment and free to the resident, and records that this was done (RR-04).
The Administrator gives all staff orientation on this policy, and again annually, including that staff must never discourage a resident from contacting the Ombudsman (STF-03).

When an Ombudsman representative arrives, any staff member greets them courteously, asks to see identification, and notifies the Administrator or the person in charge. Staff do not require advance appointments or purpose statements as a condition of entry.
The Administrator or person in charge allows the representative to enter resident areas and talk with residents who are willing to meet. Residents have the right to decline any meeting.
Staff provide a private space for conversations at the resident's request. Staff do not listen in, stay in the room, or ask the resident later what was discussed.
Staff help residents place calls, send letters, or write to the Ombudsman on request, using the resident's own phone or an establishment phone in a private place.

The person in charge releases resident records to the Ombudsman only after the Administrator confirms the legal basis, such as the resident's or representative's consent. The Administrator documents what was released, to whom, and when (RR-07).

The Administrator cooperates with Ombudsman efforts to resolve complaints. The Administrator answers Ombudsman inquiries promptly and records the contact and the outcome in the Grievance Log if the matter is a complaint (RR-02).
The Administrator reviews Ombudsman-related contacts and any access problems in the quarterly QI review and corrects any barrier immediately.
Any staff member who obstructs or retaliates against a resident for contacting the Ombudsman is subject to discipline under STF-06.

responsibilities.duty: Posts and verifies Ombudsman information, ensures access, authorizes record release, and corrects barriers.
Explains Ombudsman availability to residents and representatives at admission.
Welcome Ombudsman representatives, protect resident privacy, and never discourage contact.

documentation: Posted Ombudsman notice and the date and record of each verification
Admission checklist item confirming the Ombudsman explanation
Log of Ombudsman visits and contacts
Records-release documentation, including the consent or other authority
Staff training sign-in sheets

policies.title: Establishment Contract, Fees, Deposits and Refunds
policies.applies_to: Admissions, business office, and administrative staff of [AGENCY NAME]; all prospective residents, residents, and representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident or representative receives a complete, readable contract that meets Illinois requirements before move-in, and that fees, deposits, and refunds are handled exactly as the contract states.
policies.policy: Before a resident moves in, [AGENCY NAME] enters into a written contract with the resident or representative. The document is titled 'Assisted Living Establishment Contract' or 'Shared Housing Establishment Contract', as applicable to our license, and is printed in at least 12-point type. It contains all 20 elements required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.2030(a) and the additional terms required by subsection (b). A copy goes to the resident or representative, and the signed contract is kept on the premises throughout the residency. Fees are not changed except as the contract and this policy allow.

definitions.definition: The written agreement between the establishment and the resident or representative covering services, fees, rights, and terms of residency.
Services beyond the base rate that are listed in the contract with a fee schedule.
A documented change in the resident's services based on a change in the resident's needs, made under the service plan (ADM-03).

procedures: The Administrator maintains one approved contract template for each license type. The template is titled 'Assisted Living Establishment Contract' or 'Shared Housing Establishment Contract', set in at least 12-point type, and reviewed by legal counsel before first use and after any change in law.

The template includes all 20 elements in 295.2030(a). These include: license status; base rate and services included; extra services and fee schedule; the complaint process with notice of the Department on Aging Senior Helpline and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program; the statement that Medicaid does not pay for services in an assisted living or shared housing establishment; admission and termination criteria; the risk management statement; resident responsibilities; the Section 95 rights list and the statement that signing does not forfeit those rights; and the IDPH statement on the annual on-site review process. The Administrator uses a checklist to verify all 20 elements are present at each template review.

The template also includes the 295.2030(b) terms: fees, charges and deposits (including any charge for days of absence); the refund policy; resident responsibilities; and the policy for notifying a relative or other designated person in an emergency.

Before signing, the admissions designee gives the resident and any representative a complete copy of the draft contract and the current fee schedule, and allows time to review it and consult family, counsel, or the Ombudsman.

The designee reviews each section with the resident and representative in plain language, in the resident's preferred language, using interpretation or aids where needed (RR-08). The designee specifically explains the base rate, extra-service fees, deposits, refund rules, absence charges, termination criteria, and the Medicaid statement.

The resident or representative and the Administrator sign and date the contract before move-in. The designee confirms that all blanks are completed. No fee, charge, or deposit may be collected that is not stated in the contract.

The designee gives a complete copy of the signed contract to the resident or representative the same day it is signed and documents the date of delivery. The original is kept in the resident record, which stays on the premises for the duration of residency (REC-01).

The business office collects and records any deposit as stated in the contract and issues a written receipt. Deposits are recorded in a ledger separate from operating funds, and the Administrator reconciles them monthly.

The Administrator gives the resident or representative at least 30 days' written notice before any change in a fee or charge takes effect. The notice states the old fee, the new fee, and the effective date, and the resident or representative acknowledges receipt. No 30-day notice is required where the change results from a documented service-plan change. In that case the designee still explains the fee change and records it in the resident record.

The contract renews yearly when the contract provides for automatic renewal. Any amendment is written and signed by both parties before taking effect. The Administrator never changes terms by verbal agreement or by unilateral notice other than the fee-change notice above.

If the resident and the establishment agree to end the contract, the Administrator may end it immediately by signed mutual agreement. Terminations initiated by either side without mutual agreement follow the contract and ADM-05.

When a resident leaves, the business office calculates any refund under the contract's refund policy and provides a written, itemized statement. The refund is issued within the timeframe stated in the contract, which is [REFUND DEADLINE STATED IN CONTRACT]. A second person reviews the calculation.

The Administrator audits five percent of contract files, or at least three files, each quarter for the presence of all required elements, signatures, and delivery of copies, and reports the results to the QI committee (GOV-04). Any deficiency is corrected at once.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the contract template, fee schedule, and refund policy.
Maintains the template and checklist, signs contracts, issues fee-change notices, and audits files.
Reviews the contract with residents, obtains signatures, and delivers copies.
Collects and records deposits and fees, and calculates and issues refunds.

documentation: Contract template with the 20-element checklist and review dates
Signed contract with date of copy delivery
Current fee schedule and extra-services list
Deposit receipts and deposit ledger
30-day fee-change notices with acknowledgments
Signed amendments
Itemized refund statements
Quarterly contract audit results

policies.title: Resident Funds and Personal Property
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME], especially the business office and direct care staff; all residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To protect residents' money and belongings from loss, misuse, and exploitation, and to make sure deposits and fees are handled in line with the establishment contract.
policies.policy: Residents keep control of their own money and personal property. [AGENCY NAME] does not hold or manage a resident's personal funds unless the resident or representative requests it in writing, and then only with the safeguards below. Staff may not borrow from, sell to, accept gifts of value from, or use the money, property, or accounts of residents. Deposits and fees are handled only as the contract states (RR-04). Any suspected misuse of resident money or property is treated as possible financial exploitation under SAF-01.

definitions.definition: Cash, checks, bank accounts, cards, and other money belonging to a resident, apart from amounts owed to the establishment under the contract.
Furniture, clothing, jewelry, electronics, medical equipment, and other belongings the resident brings or acquires.
Improper use of a resident's money, property, or assets for another person's benefit. See SAF-01.

procedures: At admission, the admissions designee explains to the resident and representative that the resident keeps control of funds and property. The designee advises against keeping large amounts of cash or valuables in the room and offers use of a lockable space for valuables, as available.

Within 48 hours of move-in, the designee and the resident or representative complete a Personal Property Inventory listing valuables and significant items. Both sign it. The resident receives a copy and the original is filed in the record.
The resident or representative updates the inventory when items are added or removed. The designee dates and initials each update.

If a resident or representative asks in writing that the establishment hold funds, the Administrator reviews the request. If accepted, the Administrator signs a written agreement that states what will be held, how it will be accounted for, and how the resident can withdraw the funds at any time. Funds are held in a separate account or lockbox. They are never mixed with operating funds.

For any funds held, the business office keeps an individual ledger for each resident. Every deposit and withdrawal is recorded with the date, amount, purpose, and the signature of the resident or representative, with a receipt. A second staff member witnesses each cash transaction.
The Administrator reconciles the held funds and ledger monthly and gives each resident or representative a written statement at least quarterly.

Staff do not witness or sign legal documents for residents, handle residents' bank cards or PINs, or run personal errands involving cash, unless the Administrator has approved the arrangement in writing in advance and each transaction is receipted.

Deposits and fees owed to the establishment are collected, receipted, and refunded only in the way stated in the contract (RR-04). The business office never withholds a resident's own funds or property to collect a disputed charge.

A staff member who learns that a resident's property or money is missing reports it to the Administrator the same shift. The Administrator opens a Lost or Missing Property Report, searches the area, interviews the resident and staff, and tells the resident or representative of the findings.
If theft, misuse, or exploitation is suspected, the Administrator follows SAF-01 immediately, including required reporting to the proper agencies and, where appropriate, law enforcement.

When a resident leaves or dies, staff and the resident or representative review the Personal Property Inventory together. Property and any held funds are returned to the resident or representative with a signed receipt, with an itemized final accounting for funds. In case of death, release follows HCS-09 and applicable law.
The Administrator reviews lost property reports and fund accounting results at each quarterly QI meeting (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approves any holding of funds, reviews reconciliations, investigates missing property, and reports suspected exploitation.
Keeps ledgers and receipts, reconciles monthly, and issues statements.
Completes the personal property inventory and explains safeguards.
Do not borrow, accept gifts, or misuse resident property, and report missing items or concerns promptly.

documentation: Personal Property Inventory with updates
Written agreement and individual ledger for any funds held
Receipts and monthly reconciliations, and quarterly resident statements
Lost or Missing Property Reports and investigation notes
Discharge or death property release receipts
QI minutes showing review

policies.title: Advance Directives
policies.applies_to: Admissions staff, nursing and direct care staff, and the Administrator of [AGENCY NAME]; all residents and representatives
policies.purpose: To respect each resident's right to make decisions about medical care, including by advance directive, by asking about directives at admission, recording them, and making them available when needed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects residents' right to make their own health care decisions and to state their wishes in advance. We ask about advance directives and Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment (POLST) at pre-admission, record the answers, and keep copies in the resident record. We do not condition admission or the quality of care on whether a resident has or lacks an advance directive. Staff do not give legal advice and do not interpret medical orders on their own. Where staff are unsure what to do in an emergency, they call 911 and give the documents to emergency responders. The Administrator will have legal counsel confirm that these procedures comply with Illinois law on health care powers of attorney and POLST before publishing this policy and at each annual review.

definitions.definition: A written document, such as a health care power of attorney or living will, that states a person's health care wishes or names someone to make decisions if the person cannot.
Practitioner Orders for Life-Sustaining Treatment: a signed medical order, completed with a health care practitioner, that states a person's wishes about life-sustaining treatment.
A person designated by the resident or authorized by law to act for the resident. See RR-09.

procedures: At pre-admission screening, the admissions designee asks the prospective resident whether they have an advance directive, health care power of attorney, or POLST, and offers general written information about them. The answer is recorded on the admission checklist (ADM-01).
If the resident has one, the designee asks for a copy. The designee does not require a copy as a condition of admission or care, and does not pressure the resident to make or revoke a directive.

The designee records the document type, date, agent name and phone number, and the location of the original in the resident record. The agent is added to the contact list and, if the resident wishes, is identified as the resident's representative (RR-09).

The nurse or Administrator reviews the document with the resident at the initial assessment and checks that the resident's current wishes are consistent with it. If the resident wants to change a directive, staff suggest the resident speak with a physician or attorney and give the resident reasonable help in doing so, without giving legal advice.

The service plan notes that an advance directive or POLST exists and where the copy is kept (ADM-03). A resident who has none is asked again at each reassessment and when the resident's health condition changes (ADM-02, HCS-04).
The Administrator places a copy of any POLST or directive in a clearly labeled, quickly accessible location, such as the front of the record. Staff on every shift are told where to find it.

In an emergency, staff call 911 and begin emergency response as trained, including CPR where applicable. They give emergency responders the POLST or directive and other documents immediately on arrival. Staff do not interpret or decide on withholding care on their own. Responders and the resident's physician determine how to act on the document.
When a resident is transferred to a hospital, staff send a copy of the directive or POLST with the resident and record this in the transfer documentation (HCS-04).
The nurse or Administrator tells the resident's physician about a new or changed directive and records it in the record.
Staff treat directives as protected health information. Copies are released only as permitted by law and the resident's authorization (RR-07, 45 CFR 164.530).
At each staff orientation and annual training, the Administrator reviews this policy, including where documents are kept and what to do in an emergency (STF-03).
The Administrator audits a sample of resident records quarterly to confirm the directive question was asked and recorded, and reports findings to QI (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures legal review of this policy, maintains accessible storage, and audits records.
Asks about directives at pre-admission and records and files copies.
Reviews directives with the resident at assessment, tells the physician of changes, and keeps the service plan current.
Know where directives are kept, call 911 in an emergency, and present the documents to responders.

documentation: Admission checklist item showing the advance directive question and the response
Copies of advance directives and POLST in the resident record
Service plan notation about directives
Transfer forms showing the directive was sent with the resident
Legal counsel review record
Quarterly audit results
