Signed comprehensive assessment (Physician's Assessment Form version as confirmed with IDPH)
Written IDPH guidance on form version
Validated dementia assessment tool and physician/PA/APRN approval where applicable
Supplemental establishment assessment
Age and 55+ confirmation
Admission Checklist with date of criteria check
Signed establishment contract
Written denial notice with reasons
Admission file audit and quarterly QI review

policies.title: Resident Assessment and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment / Shared Housing Establishment (Administrator, Nurse, service plan staff, physician/PA/APRN, direct care staff)
policies.purpose: To ensure each resident's comprehensive assessment is repeated at least annually and whenever there is a significant change in condition, and that the results lead to an updated service plan.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] repeats each resident's comprehensive assessment at least annually and on a significant change in condition, including a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia. The IDPH rule may require more frequent skin-integrity and nutritional-status assessments. [AGENCY NAME] follows the current rule and performs those assessments on the schedule it sets. In a dementia program, annual and change-of-condition assessments are signed by a physician. A change in condition may be identified by a family member, staff member or the resident's physician, PA or APRN, and any staff member who learns of one reports it right away. Results of every reassessment are used to review and update the service plan (ADM-03). On request, the resident or representative receives copies of the latest assessment, any supplemental establishment assessment and the service plan.

definitions.definition: The comprehensive assessment of physical, cognitive and psychosocial condition repeated at least once every 12 months.

A major change in the resident's physical, cognitive or psychosocial status that is not expected to be short term. Examples are a new diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia, a decline in ability to perform activities of daily living, a fall with injury, new wandering or aggressive behaviors, a marked weight loss, new pressure injury, or a return from hospital with new care needs.
An additional assessment completed by [AGENCY NAME] staff to support service planning.
The dementia assessment standard that IDPH rule identifies, used for residents in a dementia program or with cognitive impairment.

procedures: The Administrator keeps an Assessment Tracking Log showing each resident's admission date, last comprehensive assessment date and the next due date. The Administrator checks the log weekly.

The Nurse sends the assessment request to the resident's physician, PA or APRN at least 45 days before the annual due date (agency standard). The Nurse tracks it to completion and files the signed assessment. The comprehensive assessment is never allowed to go past 12 months since the last one.

For residents in a dementia program, the annual assessment uses the validated dementia-specific tool, is approved as the Act requires, and is signed by a physician. The Nurse verifies the physician's signature and date before filing it.

Any staff member who notices a possible significant change in a resident's condition reports it to the Nurse or Administrator the same shift. Family members, the resident, the representative and the resident's physician, PA or APRN may also report a change, and the person receiving the report writes it in the resident record.

The Nurse evaluates the reported change the same day and decides whether it is significant. The Nurse records the evaluation and the reasons. If there is any doubt, the Nurse treats the change as significant. The Nurse notifies the physician, PA or APRN and the representative as HCS-04 requires.

A diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia is always treated as a significant change. The Administrator arranges a new comprehensive assessment, using the validated dementia-specific tool, and updates the service plan.

As an agency standard, the Nurse arranges for the change-of-condition reassessment to be completed within 7 days after the change is identified, or sooner if the resident's safety requires. For dementia program residents, a physician signs the reassessment.
The Nurse completes a supplemental establishment assessment at the same time to capture daily care needs, risk factors and resident preferences, and gives it to the assessing physician, PA or APRN.

The Administrator reviews skin-integrity and nutritional-status assessment requirements in the current rule at least annually and whenever IDPH issues a rule change. The Administrator sets the schedule in writing and updates the Assessment Tracking Log. Until the rule specifies a frequency, the Nurse checks each resident's skin (HCS-07) and weight at least monthly as an agency standard and records the results.
The Nurse reports significant skin changes, weight loss or poor food intake to the physician, PA or APRN and to the dietary manager, and the care plan is updated (DL-01).

Within 7 days after any reassessment is completed, the Nurse and Administrator review the findings with the resident and representative, and review and update the service plan (ADM-03). The resident, representative and provider agree to the revised plan, and each signs and dates it.

The Administrator compares the reassessment findings to the conditions [AGENCY NAME] cannot serve (ADM-04). If the resident's needs now exceed what the establishment can provide or secure, the Administrator starts the process in ADM-04 and ADM-05.

When a resident or representative asks for a copy of the latest assessment, any supplemental establishment assessment or the service plan, the Administrator provides copies as RR-07 requires and logs the request.

The Administrator audits the Assessment Tracking Log and a sample of reassessments quarterly, looking for late assessments, missing signatures and delays in service plan updates. The results go to the quality improvement committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the tracking log, ensures assessments are done on time, sets skin and nutrition assessment schedules from the current rule, and audits compliance.
Evaluates changes in condition, coordinates assessments with the physician, PA or APRN, completes supplemental assessments and verifies required signatures.
Completes the annual and change-of-condition comprehensive assessment; a physician signs it for dementia program residents.
Observe residents and report any change in condition to the Nurse the same shift.

documentation: Assessment Tracking Log
Signed annual and change-of-condition comprehensive assessments
Validated dementia assessment tool and physician signature (dementia program)
Change-of-condition report and Nurse evaluation
Supplemental establishment assessments
Skin-integrity and nutritional-status assessment records and weights
Updated service plan signatures
Requests for copies and dates provided
Quarterly audit results

policies.title: Service Plan
policies.applies_to: All residents of the assisted living or shared housing establishment; the Director/Manager, nursing and care staff, and anyone who delivers or supervises resident services
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident has a written service plan. The plan must be based on a current assessment and on the resident's own interests, preferences, dislikes and known triggers. It must be mutually agreed, kept current, and actually staffed, so that services match the resident's needs and the establishment contract.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will develop a written service plan for each resident from the resident's assessment and from the resident's interests, preferences, dislikes and known triggers for behavior that endangers the resident or others. The plan is mutually agreed by [AGENCY NAME], the resident and the resident's representative, if any. It will be reviewed at least annually and sooner whenever the resident's condition, preferences or needs change, and it is the basis for the services delivered under the establishment contract. A copy of the plan will be given to the resident or representative on request. [AGENCY NAME] will not put a service in a plan unless it has staff to deliver it, and it will not promise services it cannot staff or secure.

definitions.definition: The written plan, mutually agreed by the provider, the resident and the representative, that lists the services the resident will receive and how and by whom they will be delivered.

The comprehensive assessment of the resident's physical, cognitive and psychosocial condition completed by a physician, physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse before admission, and repeated at least annually and on a significant change in condition (including a diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia). Any supplemental establishment assessment is also an input to the plan.
The person the resident has designated, or who is legally authorized, to act for the resident in agreeing to the plan.
A known circumstance, person, sound, routine or condition that tends to provoke behavior that could endanger the resident or others.

A change in the resident's physical, cognitive or psychosocial status that is likely to alter the resident's needs for services, including a new diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia.

procedures: Before admission, the Director/Manager confirms that the comprehensive assessment was completed and signed by a physician, physician assistant or APRN. An assessment signed by an RN or LPN alone does not meet this requirement. The assessment is filed in the resident record.

Within the time frame set in the establishment contract and before services begin, the nurse or other qualified staff member named by the Director/Manager meets with the resident and the representative to gather the resident's interests, preferences, dislikes, daily routines, and known triggers for behavior that endangers the resident or others.

The nurse drafts the service plan from the assessment, any supplemental establishment assessment, and the preference information. The draft lists each service, how often it is given, who provides it, and whether [AGENCY NAME] provides it directly or arranges it with the resident's consent.

For each service in the draft, the Director/Manager checks that [AGENCY NAME] has enough staff with the needed skills on every shift to deliver it. Any service that cannot be staffed or secured is not placed in the plan, and the Director/Manager takes the issue to the retention review in ADM-04.

Where safety requires, the draft may provide for disconnecting or removing an appliance (for example a stove burner or a heating pad). The reason is explained to the resident and representative, written into the plan, and recorded with the resident's input.

The nurse reviews the draft with the resident and the representative, answers questions, and records any changes they ask for. The plan is final only when the provider, resident and representative all agree.
Each party signs and dates the plan, or the record notes the date and manner of agreement. The Director/Manager or designee signs for [AGENCY NAME].

The plan is placed in the resident record, and a summary of each resident's current services is made available to direct care staff in the care-instruction location kept by [AGENCY NAME] (for example, the care kardex or tablet).
The Director/Manager makes sure the services in the plan are carried over into the assignment sheets and staffing schedule, so every service has an assigned staff member and shift.
Direct care staff deliver services as written. If a service cannot be delivered as planned, staff tell the nurse or Director/Manager the same shift and record the reason.

The service plan is reviewed at least once every 12 months, and sooner when the resident's condition, preferences or needs change. Examples include a hospitalization, a fall with injury, a new diagnosis, a new or changed medication regimen, a change in cognition, or a request from the resident or representative.

When a significant change in condition occurs, the nurse notifies the Director/Manager, who arranges the repeat assessment by a physician, PA or APRN. The service plan is then revised from that assessment.
Each revision follows the same agreement steps: discuss with the resident and representative, obtain agreement, sign and date, and file. The superseded plan is retained in the record.

If service needs change because of the plan, any resulting change in fees follows the establishment contract and ADM-03 revisions are shared with the resident and representative before the new services begin. Fee changes not driven by the plan require 30 days' written notice as stated in the contract.

On request, the Director/Manager gives the resident or representative a copy of the latest assessment, any supplemental establishment assessment, and the current service plan. The date and recipient of each copy are recorded.
The Director/Manager audits a sample of service plans quarterly against the staffing schedule and delivery records. Findings are reported to the quality improvement program (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures every resident has a current, agreed, signed plan; confirms services are staffed; arranges reassessment on change in condition; approves copies released on request; audits plans quarterly.
Gathers preference and trigger information, drafts and revises plans, reviews them with residents and representatives, and updates care instructions for staff.
Deliver services according to the plan, observe and report changes in condition or preference, and report any service that cannot be delivered as planned.
Take part in developing the plan and agree to it, and tell staff when needs or preferences change.

documentation: Pre-admission comprehensive assessment signed by a physician, physician assistant or APRN
Supplemental establishment assessment, if any
Signed and dated service plan with all revisions
Record of preference, dislike and trigger interview
Documentation of any appliance disconnection or removal and its reason
Log of copies of assessment and plan given to the resident or representative
Staffing-to-plan check and quarterly audit results

policies.title: Retention Limits and Conditions the Establishment Cannot Serve
policies.applies_to: Director/Manager, nursing staff, admission staff, and all staff who observe resident condition; applies to applicants and current residents
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] admits and keeps only residents whose care needs it can safely meet with its staff and licensed services, and to prevent the penalties and harm that follow when a resident's needs exceed what the establishment is allowed or able to provide.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will not accept or retain a resident when it cannot provide or secure the care the resident needs, when it lacks staff appropriate in number and skill, or when the needed service is not one the establishment is licensed or permitted to provide. For residents in any dementia program, [AGENCY NAME] will not retain a resident whose condition has deteriorated so that residency is detrimental to the resident or others, or who is dangerous when the danger cannot be eliminated. [AGENCY NAME] will review each resident's needs against these limits at admission, at every reassessment, and on every significant change in condition. When a resident exceeds the limits, [AGENCY NAME] will start the process in ADM-05 promptly and will arrange safe transition, because caring for a resident who exceeds the care needs defined in the Act can result in a civil penalty of up to $3,000 per day.

definitions.definition: A condition under the Act or IDPH rules, or a limit of the establishment's staffing, licensure or physical plant, beyond which the establishment may not continue to care for a resident.
Staff who are sufficient in number and have the training, licensure or certification needed to deliver every service in the resident's service plan on every shift.

definitions.term: Detrimental to the resident or others
definitions.definition: A condition in which continued residency in the establishment harms, or is likely to harm, the resident or other residents, as determined through assessment and clinical review.
A resident whose behavior presents a danger to self or others that the establishment cannot eliminate through its service plan, staffing and environment.
A monetary penalty IDPH may assess: up to $5,000 per violation, each day being a separate violation, and up to $3,000 per day for caring for a resident who exceeds the care needs defined in the Act.

procedures: At pre-admission screening (ADM-01), the Director/Manager compares the applicant's assessed needs with the services [AGENCY NAME] is licensed and staffed to provide, and with the resident-eligibility criteria in the Act and IDPH rules. If the criteria are not met, the applicant is not admitted.

Before accepting any applicant, the Director/Manager confirms that staff of the number and skill needed for the applicant's care are on the schedule for every shift, and that every required service can be provided directly or secured from an outside provider with the applicant's consent.

For applicants who may have dementia, the pre-admission assessment uses a tool validated for dementia-related cognitive impairment and is approved by the physician, or by a PA or APRN with geriatric dementia experience, as required by IDPH rules.

At each annual reassessment and each reassessment for significant change (ADM-02), the Director/Manager and nurse review the new assessment against the retention limits and record the conclusion in the resident record.

Any staff member who sees a change that may place a resident outside the retention limits (for example, new need for services [AGENCY NAME] cannot provide, repeated aggression, a rapid cognitive decline, or inability to evacuate with the staff on duty) reports it to the nurse or Director/Manager the same shift.

Within 2 business days of a report, the Director/Manager and nurse hold a retention review. They consider the assessment, current service plan, incident reports, staffing, the resident's and representative's views, and input from the physician and any hospice or home health provider.

The review decides one of three outcomes: (a) the resident can still be safely served, and the service plan is revised under ADM-03; (b) a negotiated risk agreement under ADM-06 may address the specific risk, but only if the risk does not make the resident ineligible; (c) the resident can no longer be retained, and discharge or transfer begins under ADM-05.

Where a dementia program resident's condition has deteriorated so that residency is detrimental, or the resident is dangerous and the danger cannot be eliminated, the Director/Manager documents what was tried to eliminate the danger and why it failed. Annual and change-of-condition dementia assessments must be signed by a physician before the retention decision is finalized.

The Director/Manager does not use staffing shortages as a reason to leave a resident without the services in the plan. If staffing is inadequate, the Director/Manager corrects it immediately or begins the retention review.
The Director/Manager notifies the resident and representative of the review and its outcome, explains the reasons in plain language, and records the conversation.
If the resident is retained under outcome (a) or (b), the Director/Manager sets a follow-up date, no later than 30 days out, to confirm the safeguards are working.

If a resident is found to be in the establishment in violation of these limits, the Director/Manager immediately informs the governing body or owner and the legal counsel, takes steps to protect the resident and others, and begins ADM-05 without delay.
The Director/Manager keeps a log of all retention reviews and outcomes and reports a summary to the quality improvement program (GOV-04) quarterly.
The governing body reviews the log at least annually to identify patterns, such as admissions of residents who later exceed limits, and adjusts screening or staffing accordingly.

responsibilities.duty: Applies admission and retention limits, convenes retention reviews, decides outcomes with clinical input, notifies residents and representatives, and reports to the governing body.
Prepares clinical findings, reviews assessments against limits, and recommends service plan changes or discharge.
Report changes in condition and behavior promptly.
Complete and sign required assessments, including dementia-specific assessments, and advise on whether needs can be met.
Reviews retention patterns and ensures resources match the population served.

documentation: Pre-admission and reassessment documents, including validated dementia assessments and physician signatures
Retention review forms with findings, alternatives tried and outcome
Incident reports and staff change-of-condition reports linked to the review
Staffing schedule verification for each admission decision
Notices and conversation notes with resident and representative
Retention review log and quarterly QI report

policies.title: Discharge, Transfer, Relocation and Closure Notice
policies.applies_to: Director/Manager, nursing staff, business office, and all staff involved when a resident leaves, is transferred, or the establishment closes
policies.purpose: To make sure any termination of residency, transfer or relocation, or closure of the establishment is done lawfully, with written notice, the resident's rights protected, and a safe and orderly transition.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will end a residency, transfer or relocate a resident, or close the establishment only for the reasons and by the notice, procedures and appeal rights set out in the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act, IDPH's rules on termination of residency and notice of closure, and the establishment contract. The contract states the admission and residency termination criteria and procedures and how the contract may be terminated, and [AGENCY NAME] will follow them. A residency may end immediately by mutual agreement of the parties. [AGENCY NAME] will never discharge a resident as retaliation for a complaint or the exercise of rights, and will give the resident and representative written notice and help with a safe transition.

definitions.definition: The ending of a resident's right to live in the establishment, whether at the resident's request, by mutual agreement, or at the establishment's initiative under the Act, IDPH rules and the contract.
The movement of a resident to a hospital, another care setting or another unit, whether temporary or permanent.
The written notice [AGENCY NAME] must give to residents, representatives and the Department if it plans to close the establishment, within the time and by the method required by IDPH rule.
The relative or other person identified in the resident's contract to be notified in an emergency or on termination of residency.
A termination to which the resident (or representative) and [AGENCY NAME] both agree in writing, which may take effect immediately.

procedures: The Director/Manager identifies the reason for any proposed termination or transfer and confirms it matches a ground allowed by the Act, IDPH rules and the establishment contract. Reasons are limited to those stated in the contract's termination criteria.

Before issuing any notice, the Director/Manager reviews the current rule text and the signed contract, and consults legal counsel on notice periods, grounds and appeal procedures. The notice period given may never be shorter than the Act, rules and contract require.

The Director/Manager meets with the resident and representative, explains the reason, and discusses alternatives, including a revised service plan (ADM-03) or negotiated risk agreement (ADM-06) where permitted. The discussion is documented.

If the resident or representative requests to leave or agrees to leave, both parties sign a written mutual agreement stating the move-out date. An immediate termination by mutual agreement is allowed, but the resident is not pressured to agree.

For a termination at the establishment's initiative, the Director/Manager issues a written notice in plain language that states the reason, the effective date, the resident's right to appeal or dispute under the rule and contract, and the contact information for the Department on Aging Senior Helpline and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program. A copy goes to the resident and representative.
The Director/Manager notifies the relative or other designated individual named in the contract, according to the contract's notification policy, when residency is terminated.

The nurse and Director/Manager develop a transition plan with the resident and representative. It covers where the resident will go, transportation, a current medication list and supply, transfer of records the resident authorizes, and a summary of care needs for the receiving provider.

The Director/Manager helps the resident and representative find suitable alternative placements and community resources, and explains that Medicaid does not pay for services in an assisted living or shared housing establishment, as stated in the contract. Referrals are given in writing.

Emergency transfers to a hospital follow HCS-04. Notice to the representative is given immediately, and the Director/Manager decides within the period stated in the contract whether the resident can return, given retention limits in ADM-04.

The business office calculates any refund of fees, deposits or prepaid amounts under the contract and RR-04, and returns the resident's funds and personal property under RR-05 on or before move-out, with a signed receipt.

On the move-out date, a staff member and the resident or representative inventory personal belongings and medications. Medications leaving with the resident are released only with proper orders, and remaining medications are handled under HCS-01.
The Director/Manager completes the discharge record: reason, date, destination, notices given, transition plan and copies of related documents. It is filed in the resident record under REC-01.

If the establishment plans to close, the governing body decides on closure with counsel, and the Director/Manager gives written notice of closure to the Department, each resident, each representative and the Ombudsman program, within the period and by the manner required by IDPH rule.

During a closure, the Director/Manager keeps all required staffing and services in place until the last resident has safely relocated, helps each resident find a new placement, and arranges safe storage and later access to resident records as required by REC-01.
The Director/Manager reviews all involuntary discharges and closures with the governing body and the quality improvement program (GOV-04) to find ways to prevent avoidable transfers.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures lawful grounds and notice, issues written notices, supervises transition planning, and files records.
Prepares the clinical transition summary, medication reconciliation and handoff to the receiving provider.
Calculates and issues refunds, returns resident funds and property, and closes the account.
Approves any decision to close the establishment and ensures closure notices are given.
Reviews notice periods, grounds and appeal rights against current rule text before notices are issued.

documentation: Written termination notice or mutual agreement, with date and delivery method
Documentation of grounds and alternatives considered
Notification record for the designated individual or relative
Transition plan and receiving-provider handoff summary
Referral list given to resident and representative
Refund calculation, funds and property return receipts
Closure notices to the Department, residents and representatives, if applicable
Completed discharge record in the resident file

policies.title: Negotiated Risk Agreement
policies.applies_to: Director/Manager, nursing staff, residents and their representatives
policies.purpose: To give residents a structured, documented way to make informed choices that carry some risk while respecting the resident's autonomy, and to make sure [AGENCY NAME] never uses such agreements to keep a resident who is no longer eligible to reside in the establishment.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] may enter into a negotiated risk agreement with a resident when the resident chooses a course of action that carries a risk to the resident, and the risk does not make the resident ineligible for residency under the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act and IDPH rules. The agreement will be developed in line with IDPH's rules on negotiated risk and reviewed by [AGENCY NAME]'s legal counsel before the form is first used. A negotiated risk agreement will never be used to admit or keep a resident whose needs exceed what the establishment may lawfully provide, or in place of a required service.

definitions.definition: A written agreement among the resident (or representative) and [AGENCY NAME] that identifies a specific risk the resident chooses to accept, the possible consequences, the steps taken to reduce the risk, and each party's responsibilities.

A decision made by a resident with capacity (or by the representative as authorized) after the risk, its likely consequences and the alternatives have been explained in language the resident understands.
A condition or need that bars admission or continued residency under the Act and IDPH rules, or that the establishment cannot meet with its licensed services and staff.

procedures: Counsel reviews the negotiated risk agreement form against current IDPH rule text before first use, and again whenever the rule changes. The reviewed form is approved by the governing body and kept under GOV-03.

When a resident or representative asks for a choice that creates risk (for example, declining a recommended diet, refusing assistance with mobility, or choosing to continue a risky activity), staff tell the nurse the same day.
The nurse assesses the risk, reviews the resident's assessment and service plan, and tells the Director/Manager.
The Director/Manager first decides whether the risk makes the resident ineligible under ADM-04. If it does, an agreement is not used, and the retention review proceeds.

If the risk is eligible for an agreement, the nurse and Director/Manager meet with the resident and representative and explain the risk, its likely consequences and the alternatives, using plain language and any interpreter or aids the resident needs (RR-08).
The resident's physician or other practitioner is told of the proposed agreement and any clinical advice is documented.

The parties write down the specific risk, the resident's reasons, the safeguards [AGENCY NAME] will use to reduce harm, the duties of each party, how the plan will be monitored, and the date of review.
The resident (or representative), the Director/Manager and, where appropriate, the nurse sign and date the agreement. The resident receives a copy.
The service plan is updated under ADM-03 to reflect the agreement and its safeguards, and direct care staff are told their role.
Staff monitor the risk as written and report any harm, near-miss or change in condition immediately. Incidents are documented under SAF-02.
The Director/Manager reviews each agreement at least every 90 days, at each reassessment, and after any related incident. The agreement is continued, revised or ended, and the review is documented.
A resident may withdraw from the agreement at any time by telling staff. Withdrawal is documented and the service plan is revised.
If a related incident or change shows the risk is no longer one the establishment can safely manage, the Director/Manager begins the retention review in ADM-04.
The Director/Manager reports the number and nature of active agreements to the quality improvement program (GOV-04) quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether an agreement may be used, signs for [AGENCY NAME], schedules reviews, and ensures agreements are not used for ineligible residents.
Assesses the risk, explains it to the resident, drafts the agreement and monitors safeguards.
Make an informed choice, take part in drafting, and sign.
Reviews the agreement form against current IDPH rule requirements.
Carry out the safeguards and report incidents or changes.

documentation: Signed and dated negotiated risk agreement with resident copy noted
Risk assessment and eligibility check against ADM-04
Practitioner notification and advice
Updated service plan
Review notes every 90 days and after incidents
Counsel-approved form and review dates

policies.title: Medication Management, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Director/Manager, nurses, certified medication aides, direct care staff, and any staff who handle, store, remind about, supervise or dispose of resident medications
policies.purpose: To ensure medications are provided at the level of service the establishment offers and the resident chooses, are stored safely and securely, are handled only by authorized staff, and are disposed of in a documented manner.
policies.policy: The Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act defines three levels of medication service: medication reminders, supervision of self-administered medication, and medication administration. Medication services are optional services. [AGENCY NAME] offers the following levels: [SELECT THE LEVELS OFFERED: medication reminders / supervision of self-administered medication / medication administration]. Each resident's service plan states which level applies. Medications will be stored, labeled, recorded and disposed of in accordance with IDPH's rules on medications, and only staff authorized under HCS-02 will perform each level of service. Where a resident cannot open a medication container, staff may open it as part of supervised self-administration. Services may be provided directly or arranged with others with the resident's consent.

definitions.definition: A reminder to a resident that it is time to take a medication that the resident then takes without staff handling or supervising it.

Staff oversight of a resident who takes their own medication, which may include opening containers, under the direction of a licensed health care professional or, for a certified medication aide, under RN delegation and supervision.

Giving a medication to a resident by staff, which is performed by a licensed health care professional employed by the establishment or by a certified medication aide under RN supervision and delegation, within the limits in HCS-02.
Any wrong resident, drug, dose, route, time or omission, or any administration without a valid order.
A drug regulated as a Schedule II through V controlled substance.

procedures: The Director/Manager decides, with the governing body, which levels of medication service [AGENCY NAME] will offer, confirms staffing and licensure to support each level, and records the decision in this policy and in the establishment contract's service description.

At admission and at each reassessment, the nurse determines the level of medication service the resident needs and is willing to accept, based on the assessment, the resident's wishes and physician input. The level is written into the service plan (ADM-03).
The resident or representative consents in writing to medication services, including any arrangement for an outside provider or pharmacy.

On admission, the nurse obtains current medication orders from the resident's prescriber and compares them with the medications brought in. Discrepancies are resolved with the prescriber before the first dose is given by staff.

Medications received are logged by the nurse or authorized staff member with the resident name, drug, strength, quantity and date, and are labeled by the pharmacy with the resident's name and directions.

Medications are stored in a locked cabinet, drawer or cart, separate from other residents' medications and from food and cleaning products. Refrigerated medications are kept in a locked container or refrigerator at the temperature required, and temperatures are checked and logged daily.
Residents who self-administer and keep medications in their own rooms are assessed first. Medications are stored in a locked space in the room if the assessment or service plan requires it.
For medication reminders, staff remind the resident at the scheduled time and record the reminder. Staff do not handle the medication.

For supervision of self-administered medication, a staff member authorized under HCS-02 checks that the resident takes the right medication, may open containers the resident cannot open, and records what was taken, refused or missed.

For medication administration, only staff authorized under HCS-02 give medications, following the prescriber's order and the right resident, drug, dose, route and time, and record each dose immediately on the medication record.
Refusals, missed doses and errors are reported to the nurse and Director/Manager the same shift, the prescriber is notified as directed, and an incident report is completed (SAF-02).
Controlled substances are counted and signed for at each shift change by two staff members, and any discrepancy is reported to the Director/Manager immediately.

Discontinued, expired, contaminated or deceased residents' medications are removed from active storage, held in a locked area, and disposed of at least [monthly], or returned to the pharmacy, with two staff witnessing and signing a disposal record that lists drug, quantity and reason. Medications are not flushed or discarded where they can be taken by others, except as directed by the pharmacy or applicable law.

When a resident is discharged, medications that belong to the resident leave with the resident or representative only on a prescriber's order and with a signed receipt. Remaining medications are disposed of under this policy.

The Director/Manager reviews medication records, storage checks and error reports monthly and reports findings to the quality improvement program (GOV-04). A pharmacist or nurse reviews the process at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Decides and documents medication service levels offered, ensures authorized staffing, oversees storage and disposal, and reviews errors.
Determines each resident's level of service, reconciles orders, supervises and delegates under HCS-02, and monitors the medication record.

responsibilities.role: Certified medication aides and other authorized staff
responsibilities.duty: Perform only the tasks they are authorized for, document accurately, and report errors and refusals immediately.
Provide valid orders and labeling, and advise on storage, review and disposal.
Consent to the level of service and report concerns or changes.

documentation: Policy statement of medication service levels offered and the service plan entry for each resident
Resident or representative consent to medication services
Medication orders and reconciliation record
Medication administration or self-administration/reminder record
Medication receiving and inventory log
Daily refrigerator temperature log
Controlled substance count records
Disposal records with two signatures
Incident reports for medication errors and monthly review notes

policies.title: Medication Administration and Staff Authorization
policies.applies_to: Director/Manager, registered nurses, licensed practical nurses, certified medication aides, and all other direct care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure that only appropriately licensed or certified and supervised staff administer medications or supervise self-administration, within the limits of the Act and the Nurse Practice Act, and that authorization and delegation are documented.
policies.policy: Medication administration, which includes oral medications, topical treatments, eye and ear drops, nitroglycerin patches, insulin and B-12 injections, and intramuscular injections, will be performed by a licensed health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME]. A certified medication aide may administer medications only under the supervision and delegation of a registered nurse in accordance with Section 50-75 of the Nurse Practice Act, and never any Schedule II controlled substance or any subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal or intravenous medication. Supervision of self-administered medication is under a licensed health care professional or, for a certified medication aide, under RN supervision and delegation. Staff without authorization will not handle, give or supervise medications. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a current authorized-staff list with credentials and delegation records.

definitions.definition: A person licensed in Illinois to administer medications within their scope of practice, such as a registered nurse or licensed practical nurse, who is employed by the establishment.
A direct care worker who holds the required certification and may administer certain medications only under RN supervision and delegation.

An RN's written authorization, consistent with the Nurse Practice Act, for a specific task to a specific certified medication aide for a specific resident or group of residents, with ongoing supervision.
The current written list of staff permitted to give medications or supervise self-administration, with their credentials, level of authority and any limits.
Schedule II controlled substances and any subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal or intravenous medication, which a certified medication aide may not administer.

procedures: The Director/Manager and the supervising RN identify the tasks to be performed in the establishment and the staff who may perform them, and prepare the authorized-staff list. The list states for each person whether they may administer medications, supervise self-administration only, or neither.

Before authorizing any nurse to administer medications, the Director/Manager verifies the current license through the state licensing registry, records the license number and expiration date, and files a copy. The nurse must be an employee of [AGENCY NAME].

Before authorizing a certified medication aide, the Director/Manager verifies the certification and confirms the aide has completed the required training and has background and registry clearances under STF-02. Evidence is filed in the personnel record.

A registered nurse employed by or contracted with [AGENCY NAME] supervises each certified medication aide. The RN provides written delegation, naming the aide, the tasks, the residents or medication types, any limits, and the effective date, and the aide signs acknowledging it.

The RN confirms each aide's competence by direct observation before the aide first works unsupervised, and repeats observation at least [every 6 months] or after an error. Observation results are documented.

The RN reviews each resident's medication orders and marks medications that the aide may not give. Schedule II controlled substances and subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal and intravenous medications are always excluded and are given only by a licensed health care professional employed by the establishment.

If no licensed health care professional is on duty and a resident needs an excluded medication, the Director/Manager arranges a licensed professional to give it, or the prescriber is contacted for an alternative. An aide never gives an excluded medication.
Supervision of self-administration is done by a licensed health care professional or by a certified medication aide under RN delegation, following HCS-01.
At each shift, the charge nurse or Director/Manager designee checks that the staff member assigned medication duty is on the authorized-staff list. Unauthorized staff are not given medication duties.
Each administration is recorded immediately on the medication record, with the staff member's initials or signature that identifies the person who gave it.

Any error, refusal, adverse reaction or change in condition is reported to the RN or nurse on call and the Director/Manager at once, the prescriber is notified as directed, and an incident report is completed (SAF-02). The RN reviews the aide's performance after any error.
The RN may revoke or restrict a delegation at any time. The Director/Manager updates the authorized-staff list the same day and tells the aide and the shift leaders.

The Director/Manager reviews the authorized-staff list at least quarterly and each time a license or certification is renewed, suspended, revoked or expires. A staff member whose license or certification lapses is removed from medication duties immediately.
Delegation records, competency checklists and the authorized-staff list are kept on file at the establishment and are available to IDPH surveyors on request.
The Director/Manager and RN report medication administration compliance and any errors to the quality improvement program (GOV-04) monthly.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the authorized-staff list, verifies credentials, ensures only authorized staff are assigned to medication duties, and keeps delegation records on file.
Supervises and delegates to certified medication aides, assesses competence, reviews errors and may revoke delegation.

responsibilities.role: Licensed health care professionals employed by the establishment
responsibilities.duty: Administer medications within their scope of practice and give all excluded medications.
Give only delegated medications within the stated limits and report all errors and concerns promptly.
Do not handle or give medications and report medication concerns to a nurse.

documentation: Current authorized-staff list with credentials and limits
Copies of nursing licenses and medication aide certifications with verification dates
Written RN delegation for each certified medication aide, with signatures
Competency observation checklists
Medication administration records
Incident reports and RN review notes for medication errors
Quarterly authorized-staff list review and monthly QI reports

policies.title: Nursing Services and Delegation
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; all licensed nurses, certified medication aides, direct care staff, and the Director/Manager
policies.purpose: To define which nursing-related tasks [AGENCY NAME] provides, who may perform them, and how Registered Nurse (RN) supervision and delegation are carried out so that residents receive safe care and the establishment stays within Illinois law.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides nursing-related services only through staff who hold the required Illinois license or certification, and only within the scope of that license or certification. Medication administration is performed by a licensed health care professional employed by the establishment. A certified medication aide may administer medication only under the supervision and delegation of an RN in accordance with the Nurse Practice Act, and never for Schedule II controlled substances or any subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal or intravenous medication. Supervision of self-administered medication is performed by a licensed health care professional or by a certified medication aide under RN delegation. Services that [AGENCY NAME] does not provide directly may be arranged with outside providers only with the resident's consent. Before any licensed employee begins work, [AGENCY NAME] verifies the license with the Illinois professional regulation agency and files a copy in the personnel record.

definitions.definition: A prompt to a resident that it is time to take a medication that the resident self-administers, with no hands-on assistance. The term is used as defined in the Act.
Oversight of a resident who takes his or her own medication, performed by a licensed health care professional, or by a certified medication aide under RN delegation, as defined in the Act.

Giving a medication to a resident. It is performed by a licensed health care professional employed by the establishment, or by a certified medication aide under RN supervision and delegation within the limits set by law.
An RN's authorization of a specific task to a qualified person, with the RN retaining responsibility for assessment, instruction and supervision under the Nurse Practice Act.
An unlicensed staff member who holds the Illinois medication aide certification and works only under RN supervision and delegation.
A person licensed in Illinois whose scope of practice includes the task performed (for example RN or LPN).

procedures: The Director/Manager and the RN Consultant/Nurse [NURSE NAME] maintain a written list of nursing-related services [AGENCY NAME] provides directly, a list of services provided by arranged outside providers, and a list of services [AGENCY NAME] does not provide. The lists are reviewed at least annually and whenever services change.
The Director/Manager shares the lists with residents and representatives at pre-admission screening (ADM-01) and attaches the services and fee schedule to the establishment contract (RR-04).

Before an offer of employment is finalized for any position that requires a license or certification, the Director/Manager or designee verifies the license or certification online with the Illinois professional regulation agency, prints or saves the verification showing status and expiration date, and files it in the personnel record (STF-05).
No licensed or certified person performs licensed duties until the verification is filed and shows an active license without restriction that would prevent the duties assigned.

The Director/Manager or designee tracks every license and certification expiration date and re-verifies before the expiration date. A person whose license lapses is removed from licensed duties immediately until the license is shown to be active.

Medication administration is assigned only to a licensed health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME], or to a certified medication aide who has a current written RN delegation and is working under RN supervision (see HCS-02).

The RN issues delegations in writing, naming the aide, the tasks, the residents or resident groups covered, the instructions to be followed, and the supervision method. The RN reviews each delegation at least [DELEGATION REVIEW INTERVAL, e.g., every 90 days] and whenever a resident's condition or medication changes.

Certified medication aides are never assigned to administer Schedule II controlled substances or any subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal or intravenous medication. If a resident needs one of these, a licensed health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME] administers it, or the resident or representative arranges an outside provider with the resident's consent.

The RN provides on-site supervision of medication aides at the frequency set in the delegation and is reachable by phone for questions on every shift. The on-call number is posted at the medication station: [PHONE].
Staff who identify a task outside their license or delegation stop, do not perform the task, and notify the RN or Director/Manager immediately.

When a resident needs a nursing service not on the establishment's provided-services list, the RN evaluates whether [AGENCY NAME] can safely provide it or arrange it. If it cannot, the Director/Manager follows ADM-04 and HCS-04 and informs the resident and representative.
The RN reviews each resident's assessment and service plan changes (ADM-02, ADM-03) to decide whether nursing tasks, delegations or outside providers need to be added or changed.
The RN notifies the resident's physician, and the representative as required by HCS-04, when nursing observations show a change in condition.
The Director/Manager reviews delegation records, license verifications and any medication variances during the quality improvement review (GOV-04) at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Maintains the services lists, ensures licenses are verified before duties begin, ensures staffing meets the delegation requirements, and acts on any violation of scope.
Assesses residents' nursing needs, writes and reviews delegations, supervises certified medication aides, and instructs staff.
Performs only delegated tasks within legal limits, follows RN instructions, and reports problems or changes.
Do not perform nursing tasks outside their training or role, and report resident changes to the nurse.
Files license verifications and tracks expiration dates.

documentation: Written list of services provided, arranged, and not provided
License and certification verification printouts in each personnel record
License expiration tracking log
Written RN delegations and review dates
RN supervision notes
Medication aide certification copies
Quality improvement review minutes

policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; all staff, the RN/Nurse, and the Director/Manager
policies.purpose: To ensure that any change in a resident's condition is recognized, evaluated, communicated to the physician and the resident's family or designee, and acted on, including reassessment and emergency transfer to a hospital.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes and responds promptly to every change in a resident's physical, cognitive or psychosocial condition. A significant change in condition triggers a reassessment by a physician, physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse, and the service plan is reviewed and updated. For a resident with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia, the reassessment must be signed by a physician. [AGENCY NAME] notifies the resident's relative or other designated person on a significant change in condition, consistent with the emergency and relative notification policy in the establishment contract. In an emergency, staff call 911 first. Incident reporting follows the timeframes set in SAF-02 and REC-02.

definitions.definition: Any new or worsening sign, symptom, behavior, functional decline, injury or other departure from a resident's usual state.

A change that is not expected to resolve quickly, that affects more than one area of function or health, or that changes the care or services the resident needs, including a new diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia. The RN decides, with the Director/Manager, when a change is significant.
The relative, representative or other person the resident has named in the establishment contract to be contacted in an emergency or on a change in condition.
A comprehensive reassessment of physical, cognitive and psychosocial condition performed by a physician, physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse after a significant change.

procedures: Any staff member who notices a change in a resident's condition reports it to the nurse on duty, or to the shift lead if no nurse is on site, immediately and no later than the end of the shift in which it is observed. Life-threatening changes are reported at once.

If a resident is unresponsive, not breathing, has chest pain, stroke signs, severe bleeding, a serious injury or any condition that appears life threatening, staff call 911 immediately, start CPR (by CPR-certified staff) unless a valid do-not-resuscitate order or advance directive applies (RR-06), and notify the nurse and Director/Manager.
For non-emergency changes, the nurse or trained staff member observes the resident, takes vital signs when appropriate, and records what was observed on the change-of-condition form.

The nurse or designee notifies the resident's physician (or PA/APRN) the same day for any change that may need medical evaluation, and immediately for urgent changes. The notification and any orders received are recorded with date, time, the name of the person notified, and the response.
Staff follow physician orders and update the medication administration and treatment records. Verbal orders are written down, read back, and signed according to the physician's requirements.

The nurse or Director/Manager notifies the resident's designated person, relative or representative of any significant change in condition, any injury, any hospital transfer, and any new physician order that changes care. Notice is given promptly and the same day whenever possible. The call is documented with the time, the person reached, and the information given. If the person cannot be reached, staff try again and document each attempt.
The Director/Manager is notified of every significant change, emergency transfer, injury and incident on the same shift. Reportable incidents are handled under SAF-02 and REC-02.

The RN and Director/Manager decide whether the change is significant. If so, the Director/Manager arranges a reassessment by a physician, physician assistant or advanced practice registered nurse, using the validated dementia-specific tool for residents with dementia, and has it completed without delay.

For a resident with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia, the reassessment is reviewed and signed by a physician. A reassessment not signed by a physician is incomplete and is not filed as final.

After the reassessment, the RN revises the service plan with the resident and representative and reviews whether the resident still meets retention criteria (ADM-04). If the establishment can no longer meet the resident's needs, the Director/Manager starts the process in ADM-05.

For hospital transfer, staff send the resident with the face sheet, current medication list, allergies, physician and designated-person contact information, advance directive or code status, and a written summary of the reason for transfer. A staff member stays with the resident until emergency personnel arrive when staffing permits, without leaving the building uncovered.
The designated person is notified of the transfer and the receiving hospital. The nurse or Director/Manager calls the hospital within [HOURS] hours to confirm arrival and to obtain updates.

Before a resident returns from the hospital or a skilled nursing stay, the RN obtains discharge orders and medication changes, determines whether a reassessment is needed, and confirms that [AGENCY NAME] can meet the resident's needs. The service plan is updated before or on the day of return.
The nurse reviews each shift report and the 24-hour log for changes that were not reported, and follows up with the staff involved.
Change-of-condition trends, transfers, and readmissions are reviewed in the quality improvement program (GOV-04) at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Observe and promptly report changes, call 911 in an emergency, and document what they saw.
Evaluates changes, notifies physicians, determines whether a change is significant, and updates the service plan.
Arranges reassessments, ensures family notification occurs, handles incident reporting, and decides on retention questions.
Evaluates the resident, gives orders, and completes the reassessment; a physician signs reassessments for residents with dementia.
Receives notice and takes part in service plan decisions.

documentation: Change-of-condition form
Physician/PA/APRN notification log and orders
Designated-person notification log with attempts
Reassessment report signed by the required professional (physician signature for dementia residents)
Updated service plan
Hospital transfer sheet and return documentation
Incident report where applicable
Quality improvement trend report

policies.title: Dementia and Memory Care
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment that admits or retains residents with Alzheimer's disease or related dementia, or offers a special dementia program or unit
policies.purpose: To make sure that residents with dementia are assessed with a validated tool, receive safe care and meaningful activity, that the establishment makes required disclosures, and that staff are trained and sufficient in number.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] admits or retains a resident with Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia only if it can provide or secure appropriate care and has appropriately skilled staff. A resident is not admitted or retained if the resident's condition has deteriorated so that residency is detrimental to the resident or others, or if the resident is dangerous and the danger cannot be eliminated. Residents with dementia are assessed with a validated dementia-specific tool before acceptance, annually, and on a change in condition; annual and change-of-condition assessments are signed by a physician. [AGENCY NAME] files the Alzheimer's disease and related dementias special care disclosure document with IDPH as a condition of licensure. If [AGENCY NAME] offers a special dementia program or unit, it also meets every requirement of Section 150 of the Act, and all other provisions of the Act apply as well. [AGENCY NAME] does not describe itself as a separate licensed memory care category, because Illinois does not license one.

definitions.definition: A program or unit that [AGENCY NAME] holds out as providing special care to residents with Alzheimer's disease or related dementia.
The document required by the Alzheimer's Disease and Related Dementias Special Care Disclosure Act, filed with IDPH and given to prospective and actual residents.
A cognitive and functional assessment tool identified by IDPH rule that is validated for dementia-related cognitive impairment and has inter-rater reliability.
The person who acts for a resident with dementia in decisions and communications, ensured by the establishment (RR-09).
Movement by a resident with cognitive impairment that puts the resident at risk, including leaving the building or grounds unsupervised.

procedures: The Director/Manager decides, before accepting any admission, whether [AGENCY NAME] will serve residents with dementia and whether it will operate a special dementia program or unit. The decision is recorded in the admission criteria (ADM-01) and the licensure file.

If [AGENCY NAME] serves residents with dementia, the Director/Manager completes the special care disclosure document, files it with IDPH as a condition of licensure, updates it whenever the program changes, and keeps the filed copy in the licensure file (GOV-02).

The Director/Manager gives the disclosure document to every prospective resident and representative before the contract is signed, and to current residents or representatives whenever it changes. Receipt is signed and filed.

Before acceptance, a physician, or a PA or APRN with geriatric dementia experience, approves a pre-admission assessment using the validated dementia-specific tool. The tool must be validated for dementia-related cognitive impairment. Results are reviewed with the resident and representative.

The Director/Manager and RN determine from the assessment whether [AGENCY NAME] can provide or secure appropriate care with appropriately skilled staff, and whether any danger posed by the person can be eliminated. If not, the person is not admitted, and the Director/Manager gives the applicant and representative a written explanation and referral suggestions (ADM-04).

The annual assessment and any assessment after a change in condition use the validated dementia-specific tool and are signed by a physician. The Director/Manager tracks the due date of each resident's assessment and schedules it at least 30 days ahead.
A new diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease or a related dementia is a significant change in condition and triggers a reassessment (HCS-04).

For each resident with dementia, the Director/Manager ensures that a designated representative is identified and recorded (RR-09). Where a resident has none, the Director/Manager documents efforts to obtain one and informs the resident about options.

The service plan for each resident with dementia (ADM-03) addresses cognition, communication, behaviors, nutrition and hydration, toileting, sleep, safety, and the resident's preferences and life history, and lists specific approaches for staff to use.
The Activities Coordinator offers daily cognitive stimulation and activities suited to the stage of dementia, including structured and individual options, and records resident participation (DL-02).

The Director/Manager adopts and follows written policies for the continued safety of all residents, including residents who may wander and residents who need help evacuating. These include wandering risk screening on admission and change of condition, regular visual checks, door and exit safeguards that comply with life safety rules, and the elopement response in SAF-03 and the evacuation procedures in SAF-05 and SAF-06.
Restrictive practices, including locked doors, alarms and any restraint, are used only as permitted under SAF-04 and the fire safety requirements, and are never used for staff convenience.

The Director/Manager sets staffing patterns for the dementia program by shift, based on resident acuity, and verifies they meet the staffing requirements in the current IDPH rule for Alzheimer and dementia programs. The Director/Manager confirms the current rule requirements before opening the program and at each annual policy review.

The Director/Manager and all direct care staff complete dementia training that meets the content and hours in the current IDPH rule. The Director/Manager completes it before the program starts, and direct care staff complete it during orientation or before working independently with residents with dementia, and then annually or as the rule requires (STF-03). Completion is filed in each personnel record.

Staff communicate with family members of residents with dementia on admission, at each service plan review, and on any change in condition or incident. Staff record these contacts. The Director/Manager holds a family meeting at least [FREQUENCY] to discuss the program.
The emergency procedures and emergency staffing patterns for the dementia program are written into the emergency plan (SAF-05) and reviewed at each annual plan review and drill.
The QI committee reviews dementia program data, including falls, elopement attempts, behaviors, weight loss, transfers and discharges (GOV-04), at least quarterly.

responsibilities.duty: Files the disclosure document, ensures assessments, representatives, staffing and training are in place, and decides on admission and retention with the RN.
Coordinates assessments with the physician, writes and updates the service plan, and trains and guides staff.
Approves the pre-admission assessment and, for annual and change-of-condition assessments, a physician signs.
Plans and documents cognitive stimulation and activities.
Use the care approaches in the service plan, supervise residents, and report changes and wandering.

documentation: Special care disclosure document as filed with IDPH and proof of receipt by residents
Validated assessment results with physician or PA/APRN approval and physician signature on annual and change-of-condition assessments
Designated representative records
Service plans for residents with dementia
Activity participation logs
Wandering and evacuation policies and drill records
Staffing pattern schedules
Director and staff dementia training records
Family communication logs
QI dementia program reports

policies.title: Falls Prevention
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; all direct care staff, nursing staff, maintenance staff, and the Director/Manager
policies.purpose: To reduce falls and fall-related injuries by identifying residents at risk, putting individualized prevention measures in the service plan, responding to falls correctly, and tracking falls for quality improvement.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] works to prevent falls while respecting each resident's right to make choices and live as independently as possible. Fall risk is identified at assessment, addressed in the service plan, and reviewed after every fall and on any change in condition. Every fall is reported, documented and followed up. Falls are tracked and analyzed in the quality improvement program. No Illinois assisted living rule prescribes a single falls program, so this policy is carried out through the assessment, service plan, incident reporting and quality improvement processes the establishment already follows.

definitions.definition: An unplanned descent to the floor or other lower surface, with or without injury, whether witnessed or not, including a resident found on the floor.

Conditions that raise the chance of falling, such as prior falls, unsteady gait, weakness, dizziness, medications, vision problems, cognitive impairment, urinary urgency, footwear and environmental hazards.
A review done after each fall to find the cause and change the plan.

procedures: At admission and at each assessment, the RN or Director/Manager records each resident's fall history and risk factors using the facility fall risk screen, and shares the result with the resident, the representative and the physician or PA/APRN who completes the assessment (ADM-02).

The service plan lists specific fall prevention measures for each resident at risk, such as assistive devices, scheduled toileting, standby assistance for transfers, footwear, call-system access, lighting, and exercise or physical therapy, and is agreed with the resident and representative (ADM-03).

The RN reviews each resident's medication list with the pharmacist or physician when a resident has a fall or starts a medication known to increase fall risk, and asks the physician to review medications that may be contributing.
A resident who chooses to decline a recommended safety measure is offered a negotiated risk agreement (ADM-06) so that the risk and the choice are discussed and documented.

Maintenance and housekeeping staff inspect hallways, common areas, bathrooms and grounds for hazards at least daily, including loose rugs, spills, clutter, poor lighting, uneven surfaces, wet floors and ice, and correct hazards at once or block off the area (SAF-10, DL-03).

Direct care staff check that call systems, grab bars, handrails, beds, chairs and wheelchairs work, that brakes are working, and that residents have their glasses, hearing aids and walkers in reach. Defects are reported to maintenance the same day.

When a fall occurs, staff stay with the resident, do not move the resident if injury is suspected, and call the nurse. For a serious injury, a suspected fracture, head injury with a change in alertness, or other emergency, staff call 911 and follow HCS-04.

The nurse or trained staff member checks the resident, including vital signs and signs of injury, and observes a resident who hit the head or is on blood thinners at intervals set by the nurse or physician, for at least [OBSERVATION PERIOD] hours, with written entries.

The nurse notifies the physician or PA/APRN and the resident's designated person according to HCS-04 and completes an incident report under SAF-02 before the end of the shift. Reportable events are reported to the state within the required timeframes (REC-02).

Within [TIMEFRAME, e.g., 72 hours] of each fall, the nurse and care team complete a post-fall review that looks at time, place, activity, footwear, medications, toileting, environment and resident condition, and record changes to the service plan.

The Director/Manager makes sure that a resident with repeated falls, or a fall with a significant injury, receives a reassessment and a service plan review (HCS-04) and considers whether physical therapy or another outside provider should be arranged with the resident's consent.
New direct care staff receive training on fall prevention, safe transfers and assisting residents with walking in orientation, with refresher training at least annually (STF-03).

The QI coordinator records every fall in the falls log and prepares a monthly summary by resident, time of day, location and injury. The QI committee reviews trends at least quarterly, sets goals, and follows up on corrective actions (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Carry out fall prevention measures, supervise and assist residents as planned, remove hazards, and report falls immediately.
Screens fall risk, evaluates residents after falls, completes post-fall reviews, and revises service plans.
Inspect and correct environmental hazards and repair safety equipment.
Ensures follow-up, training, reporting and incident documentation, and presents data to the QI committee.
Take part in planning and tell staff about concerns or changes.

documentation: Fall risk screen and fall history in the assessment
Service plan fall prevention measures
Incident reports
Post-fall observation notes
Post-fall review forms
Physician and designated-person notification records
Environmental inspection logs
Monthly falls log and QI committee minutes
Staff fall prevention training records

policies.title: Skin Integrity
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; nursing staff, direct care staff, and the Director/Manager
policies.purpose: To prevent pressure injuries and other skin breakdown, detect skin problems early, and make sure residents receive the right assessments, treatments and outside care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] helps residents keep healthy skin through prevention, regular observation and prompt response. The Act allows IDPH to set by rule circumstances that require more frequent skin integrity and nutritional status assessments. [AGENCY NAME] will do skin integrity and nutritional status assessments at least as often as required by the current IDPH rule, and will confirm the current rule text before setting or changing its frequency. Skin problems are reported to the nurse and the physician, and [AGENCY NAME] follows the retention limits in ADM-04 if a resident's skin care needs exceed what the establishment can provide or secure.

definitions.definition: Localized damage to skin and underlying tissue, usually over a bony area, caused by pressure or pressure with shear.
A documented head-to-toe inspection of the skin by a licensed nurse that notes color, temperature, moisture, intact or broken areas, and risk factors.
A documented review of weight, intake, appetite, swallowing, diet and risk of weight loss or dehydration.

procedures: At admission and at every comprehensive assessment, the RN checks the resident's skin and records the result and any existing wounds, with dates and location, in the record (ADM-02). The nurse also records skin risk factors such as immobility, incontinence, poor nutrition, diabetes and circulation problems.

Before a rule-based frequency is set, the Director/Manager confirms the current IDPH rule text on skin integrity and nutritional status assessment frequency and records the rule date and requirement in the policy file. The facility's schedule must be at least as frequent as the rule requires; the Director/Manager rechecks the rule at each annual policy review (GOV-03).

The RN performs a skin integrity assessment and a nutritional status assessment on the schedule set under step 2, and sooner when a resident has a significant change in condition, a new wound, a hospital stay, weight loss or a decline in eating or mobility.

The service plan lists skin protection measures for residents at risk, such as repositioning schedules, pressure-reducing cushions or mattresses ordered by a physician, continence care, moisture control, nutrition and fluids, and footwear, and is agreed with the resident and representative (ADM-03).

Direct care staff look at the resident's skin during bathing, dressing and toileting, and report redness that does not fade, blisters, open areas, swelling, bruises, skin tears, heel or ankle pain, or any new area of concern to the nurse the same shift.

The nurse examines any reported area promptly, documents location, size, color, drainage and pain, and notifies the physician or PA/APRN the same day for any open area, suspected pressure injury or signs of infection. The designated person is notified under HCS-04.

Treatment of wounds is done only by staff licensed to perform it, or by home health or other outside providers arranged with the resident's consent and coordinated with the establishment (HCS-08). Staff follow physician orders and record each treatment.

The RN weighs each resident on admission and at least monthly, or more often when ordered, and reports unplanned weight loss or poor intake to the physician and the dietary staff for review of diet and supplements (DL-01).
Staff encourage and help residents with fluids, meals and movement, and offer repositioning to residents who cannot change position by themselves, as set out in the service plan.

The RN and Director/Manager decide whether a resident with a pressure injury or complex wound can still be served. If the wound or care needed is beyond what the establishment can provide or secure with appropriately skilled staff, the Director/Manager follows ADM-04 and ADM-05.
New direct care staff are trained on skin observation, repositioning, incontinence care and reporting during orientation, with refresher training at least annually (STF-03).
Skin injuries are tracked monthly by the QI coordinator, including newly acquired pressure injuries, and reviewed in the QI program at least quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Performs skin and nutritional assessments, examines reported areas, notifies the physician, and updates the service plan.
Observe and report skin changes and carry out prevention measures in the service plan.
Confirms the current IDPH rule on assessment frequency, ensures follow-up, and decides on retention with the RN.
Provide diets and supplements as ordered and report poor intake.
Evaluates wounds and gives treatment and equipment orders.
