Nutritional status assessments and weight records
Record of the IDPH rule text and date checked
Service plan skin protection measures
Wound documentation and treatment records
Physician and designated-person notification records
Staff training records
Monthly skin injury tracking log and QI minutes

policies.title: Hospice and Home Health Coordination
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Establishment and Shared Housing Establishment; the Director/Manager, nursing staff, direct care staff, and outside hospice and home health providers serving residents
policies.purpose: To coordinate care between [AGENCY NAME] and hospice and home health agencies, protect each resident's right to choose providers, and ensure that the establishment continues to meet its own responsibilities and limits.
policies.policy: Residents may receive services from hospice, home health and other providers that [AGENCY NAME] does not contract with, and the establishment contract says so. Services may be provided by third parties arranged with the resident's consent. The contract also describes the license status of every provider of health-related or supportive services that [AGENCY NAME] arranges. Hospice or home health involvement does not change [AGENCY NAME]'s admission and retention limits; the establishment re-checks whether it can continue to serve the resident at each change in condition. Medication administration and supervision of self-administered medication remain under the requirements of HCS-02 and HCS-03 regardless of which agency is involved.

definitions.definition: A health-related or supportive service provided by an outside provider that [AGENCY NAME] arranges with the resident's consent.
A hospice, home health or other provider chosen by the resident or representative, even though [AGENCY NAME] has no contract with that provider.
Sharing information and dividing duties among the establishment, outside providers, the physician and the resident or representative so that care is consistent and safe.
An outside licensed provider of palliative and end-of-life care to a resident who has elected hospice.

procedures: The Director/Manager makes sure each establishment contract includes the statement that residents may receive services from providers with whom [AGENCY NAME] has no contract, and a description of the license status of every provider of health-related or supportive services that [AGENCY NAME] arranges (RR-04).

At pre-admission and whenever services change, staff tell the resident and representative that they may choose their own hospice or home health provider, and that [AGENCY NAME] may be able to suggest providers if asked. Staff do not require the use of any particular agency as a condition of residency.
Before arranging any outside service, the Director/Manager obtains the resident's consent (or the representative's, if the resident cannot consent) and records it in the resident record.

Before an arranged agency begins services, the Director/Manager verifies that the agency's required Illinois license is current, records the license information in the provider file, and informs the resident of the license status of the provider.

For any outside agency entering the building, whether arranged or resident-selected, the Director/Manager obtains the agency's contact information, the names of the clinicians and the agency's after-hours number, and gives the agency [AGENCY NAME]'s visitor sign-in and infection control rules, emergency and evacuation information, and contact numbers: [PHONE].

The RN meets or speaks with the hospice or home health nurse at the start of services and agrees in writing, using a coordination-of-care form, on who does what, including medication management and who gives, supervises or reminds about each medication; wound or other treatments; equipment; personal care; and who is called after hours and for emergencies.

The agreed plan is added to the resident's service plan after review with the resident and representative (ADM-03). The RN checks that the agency's plan of care and [AGENCY NAME]'s service plan do not conflict.

Staff who give medications or help with self-administration follow HCS-02 and HCS-03, and never exceed their legal scope when following hospice or home health instructions. Hospice medications and comfort kits are received, stored, recorded and disposed of under HCS-01.

Direct care staff record observations and share changes in the resident's condition with the nurse, who passes them to the hospice or home health nurse and the physician under HCS-04. The nurse records each exchange.
The RN reviews each hospice or home health visit note or summary when received and files it in the resident record.

With each change in condition, and at least at each service plan review, the Director/Manager and RN re-check whether [AGENCY NAME] can continue to serve the resident and still meets the admission and retention limits in ADM-04. The RN records the findings. If the limits are no longer met, the Director/Manager starts ADM-05 and works with the outside agency, the physician and the family on a safe plan.

When a resident is nearing death, the RN coordinates with the hospice team, the family and the physician about comfort, spiritual and cultural wishes, the advance directive (RR-06) and notifications, and the establishment follows HCS-09 at the time of death.

If a resident, representative or staff member has a concern about an outside agency, it is handled under RR-02. The Director/Manager may bring concerns to the agency and, if needed, to the appropriate regulator.
Information is shared with outside providers only as permitted by RR-07 and the resident's authorization.
The Director/Manager reviews outside provider coordination, including problems and delays, at the QI review at least quarterly (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures contract language and consent, verifies provider licenses, re-checks retention, and handles concerns about providers.
Coordinates the care plan with hospice and home health nurses, reviews visit notes, and updates the service plan.
Follow the coordinated plan within their scope, and report changes.
Delivers its services, communicates changes, and follows the establishment's building and safety rules.
Chooses providers, gives consent, and takes part in planning.

documentation: Establishment contract language on outside providers and license status
Resident or representative consent to arranged services
Provider license verification and agency contact list
Coordination-of-care form
Updated service plan
Hospice and home health visit notes
Communication log with outside providers
Retention re-check records
QI review minutes

policies.title: Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME], including direct care staff, nursing, the Administrator and business office staff, at both assisted living and shared housing sites
policies.purpose: To make sure that when a resident dies, the death is handled with dignity, that the right people are notified promptly, and that property, funds and records are handled lawfully and according to the establishment contract.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will respond to every death with respect for the resident, the resident's family and other residents. Staff will follow the resident's advance directives and hospice plan and will notify the relative or other individual designated in the resident's establishment contract. Where the law requires, staff will notify the physician, coroner or medical examiner and the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH). Personal property will be inventoried and released, and fees will be refunded, according to the resident's contract and its refund terms. Any report to IDPH will follow the Department's current rules. The Administrator will check those rules at least annually and whenever IDPH issues new guidance, and will keep the current requirement on file with this policy. Where a rule sets a shorter timeframe than this policy, the rule controls.

definitions.definition: The relative or other person named in the resident's establishment contract, under the contract's emergency and relative notification policy, to be notified of a death or emergency.
A death from a known terminal condition, usually under hospice care, where the physician or hospice has a plan in place for pronouncement and release of the body.
A death that is sudden, unattended, accidental, suspicious, or not explained by a known condition under a physician's care. It may require coroner or medical examiner notification.
The person who acts for the resident under a power of attorney, guardianship or other lawful authority, as described in the Resident's Representative policy (RR-09).

procedures: The staff member who finds a resident unresponsive immediately checks the advance directive status (POLST, DNR or other order) in the resident's chart. If there is no valid order declining resuscitation, the staff member calls 911 and starts CPR if trained and able, per HCS-04.
The staff member notifies the Administrator or the on-call manager and the nurse (if one is on duty or on call) immediately, and stays with the resident until help arrives.

For an expected death under hospice, staff call the hospice agency, which pronounces the death and directs release of the body. For other deaths, EMS or the physician pronounces the death. Staff document the time and the name of the person who pronounced it.
The Administrator or designee notifies the resident's physician or the physician's covering provider as soon as possible, and no later than the same shift.

If the death is unexpected, accidental, suspicious, or the resident had no attending physician, the Administrator notifies the county coroner or medical examiner as required by law. Staff do not disturb the room, equipment or items near the resident until released, unless needed for emergency care.
If there is any indication of abuse, neglect, exploitation or an accident, the Administrator treats the death as a reportable incident and follows SAF-01 and SAF-02.

The Administrator or designee notifies the relative or designated individual named in the contract by telephone as soon as possible after the death, in person or by phone, not by text or voicemail alone. If there is no answer, staff keep trying the contacts on file and document each attempt with the time and the result.
The Administrator or designee notifies the resident's representative, if different from the designated individual, and any case manager, hospice team, home health provider or other outside provider.
The Administrator reviews the current IDPH reporting requirements and files any required report to IDPH within the required timeframe. A copy is kept in the incident file. See REC-02.

Staff arrange release of the body to the funeral home named by the family or representative, and record the funeral home, the time of release and the staff member present. Staff ensure privacy, and screen the route where possible, during removal.

Within 24 hours, two staff members, one of them a manager, make a written inventory of the resident's personal property and secure the room. The inventory is checked against the admission inventory and any later additions.

Staff dispose of the resident's medications according to the Medication Management, Storage and Disposal policy (HCS-01). Disposal is witnessed and recorded, and controlled substances are counted and handled as that policy requires.

The Administrator releases the personal property only to the person who has legal authority to receive it, such as the representative, executor or administrator of the estate, and obtains a signed receipt. The Administrator holds any questioned items and seeks guidance rather than releasing them informally.

The business office closes the resident's account, reconciles any resident funds held under RR-05, and calculates the final charges and any refund of fees or deposits according to the refund terms in the resident's contract. The business office issues the refund to the estate or the person entitled to it, with an itemized statement, within the period stated in the contract.

The Administrator offers support to staff and to other residents, and may hold a remembrance or notice according to the wishes of the family and residents. The Administrator does not share the cause of death or other health information with other residents or visitors.

The nurse or Administrator completes the death record in the resident's chart, including the circumstances, the time found, actions taken, people notified and the times. The record is closed and retained under REC-01.
The Quality Improvement Committee reviews deaths each quarter for patterns and process issues, such as a delayed change-of-condition response, under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Check the advance directive status, call 911 when required, stay with the resident, notify the manager or nurse, and document what they saw and did.
Coordinate with hospice and the physician, complete clinical documentation, and oversee medication disposal.
Make required notifications to the family, coroner or medical examiner and IDPH, ensure the property inventory and release are done, and keep current reporting requirements on file.
Close the account and issue refunds according to the contract.
Review deaths for trends and process improvements.

documentation: Death record in the resident's chart
Advance directive or POLST on file
Notification log with the names, times and results of calls
Coroner or medical examiner notification record, if applicable
IDPH report copy, if applicable
Personal property inventory and signed release receipt
Medication disposal record
Final account statement and refund record
Quality Improvement Committee review notes

policies.title: Mandatory Services
policies.applies_to: [AGENCY NAME] management, nursing and direct care staff, and any outside providers arranged to deliver services to residents
policies.purpose: To ensure [AGENCY NAME] provides every service the Illinois Department of Public Health requires of a licensed establishment, to make clear who delivers each one, and to confirm that staffing is sufficient to cover them.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] will provide all mandatory services required by the Assisted Living and Shared Housing Act and the Department's rules for an establishment of its type, and may also offer optional services. The Administrator will keep a Mandatory Services Matrix that lists each required service exactly as it appears in the current Department rule. The matrix names who is responsible for each service, how the service is staffed and where it is documented. Services may be delivered directly by [AGENCY NAME] or by others arranged for the resident with the resident's consent. [AGENCY NAME] stays responsible for making sure the services in the contract and service plan are delivered. Staffing will be enough to cover mandatory services, services in each resident's service plan, environmental services, food service if offered, and emergency evacuation. Medication-related services will be delivered only by staff who are authorized for them under the Act, and as described in HCS-01 and HCS-02.

definitions.definition: A service that the Department's rules require every establishment of the applicable type to provide, as listed in the Department's current rule text.
A service offered beyond the mandatory list, described in the contract with its fee schedule.
A service delivered by an outside provider that [AGENCY NAME] coordinates with the resident's consent, such as home health, hospice or therapy.

definitions.term: Medication reminder, supervision of self-administered medication and medication administration
definitions.definition: Three distinct levels of medication help defined in the Act. Which staff may provide each level depends on their license or authorization, as described in HCS-02.
The Administrator's document that lists each required service, who provides it, the staffing assigned, and where it is documented.

procedures: Before opening, and at least annually after that, the Administrator obtains the current list of mandatory services from the Department's rule text and builds or updates the Mandatory Services Matrix. The Administrator dates the matrix and records the source of the text used.

For each mandatory service, the matrix identifies the responsible role, the shift coverage, the documentation location and the policy that governs it. Where a service is delivered through an outside provider, the matrix names the provider.

The Administrator confirms that no mandatory service is left out of the resident contract, and that the contract describes the base rate and services and lists extra services with a fee schedule. See RR-04.

During pre-admission screening and assessment, the nurse or other qualified person identifies the services each applicant needs and confirms [AGENCY NAME] can deliver them. If it cannot provide or arrange for appropriate care, it does not admit the applicant. See ADM-01 and ADM-04.
The service plan for each resident lists the mandatory and other services the resident will receive, how often, and who provides them. The plan is developed and updated under ADM-03.

When a resident needs a service that [AGENCY NAME] does not provide directly, the nurse or Administrator discusses options with the resident or representative, and arranges the service only with the resident's consent. The consent is documented.

Medication services are limited to what each staff member is allowed to do. Only a licensed health care professional employed by [AGENCY NAME] may administer medication. A certified medication aide may administer only under the delegation and supervision of a registered nurse, and not Schedule II controlled substances or any subcutaneous, intramuscular, intradermal or intravenous medication. Supervision of self-administered medication is performed under a licensed health care professional, or under RN delegation to a certified medication aide.

The Administrator builds each month's schedule so that sufficient qualified staff are on duty to meet scheduled and unscheduled needs 24 hours a day. Staffing must cover mandatory services, service-plan services, environmental services, food service if offered, and emergency evacuation. See STF-01.

The Administrator checks that the schedule includes at least one direct care staff person on duty at all times with current adult CPR certification, and at least one staff member awake, on duty and on site 24 hours a day (assisted living), or at least one staff member on site at all times (shared housing).
Direct care staff document each service they deliver in the resident's service record at the time of delivery, or before the end of the shift.

The nurse reviews service documentation at least weekly for missing entries and for services refused, and follows up with the resident and staff. Repeated refusals or missed services are reported to the Administrator.

Each quarter, the Quality Improvement Committee compares a sample of service-plan services against the documentation to check that the service was delivered as planned, and tracks complaints about services under GOV-04.
When the Department revises its rules, the Administrator updates the matrix, retrains affected staff within 30 days and records the update date.
Before any change in the services offered, or any fee change for a service, the Administrator updates the contract and gives residents written notice as the contract and rules require. See RR-04.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the Mandatory Services Matrix, ensure staffing covers each service, and ensure contracts match the services offered.
Assess service needs, develop and update service plans, oversee delegation and monitor service documentation.
Deliver assigned services within their authorized scope and document them.
Keep fee schedules for optional services consistent with the contract.
Audit service delivery and review complaints.

documentation: Mandatory Services Matrix with the date and source of the rule text
Service plans
Daily service and task records
Resident consent for arranged services
Staffing schedules
Delegation records for medication services
Quality Improvement audit results

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Financial Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, volunteers, contractors and agency staff of [AGENCY NAME] who have contact with residents or their funds, property or records
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect and financial exploitation by screening who is hired, training staff, responding to concerns at once, reporting to the right authorities, and investigating every allegation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, financial exploitation and misappropriation of resident property. Every employee, volunteer and contractor must report a suspicion immediately, and retaliation against anyone who reports in good faith is prohibited. [AGENCY NAME] will not hire anyone with a finding of abuse, neglect or misappropriation of property on the Illinois Nurse Aide Registry, and will screen all staff who have or may have resident contact under the Health Care Worker Background Check Act, as described in STF-02. Every allegation will be reported to the authorities required by law, the resident will be protected right away, and the Administrator will investigate. Reporting recipients, timeframes and contents follow the Department's rules and Illinois law, including the Adult Protective Services Act, and where they set a shorter timeframe than this policy, they control. Staff must follow this policy even if the reporter is unsure the event is abuse.

definitions.definition: Any physical, mental or sexual injury or harm to a resident, including hitting, rough handling, threats, humiliation, isolation, intimidation or sexual contact of any kind.
A failure to provide the care, supervision, food, medication, hygiene or services a resident needs, whether or not it is intentional.
Using a resident's money, property or assets without consent or by deception, pressure or undue influence, including borrowing, accepting gifts or taking items.
Deliberately taking, misplacing or using a resident's belongings or funds without permission.
The state registry that records findings of abuse, neglect or misappropriation of property against certified nurse aides and other individuals.
A person who must report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation under Illinois law. [AGENCY NAME] treats all staff as reporters under this policy.

procedures: Before an offer of employment takes effect, the Administrator checks the Illinois Nurse Aide Registry and does not hire anyone with a finding of abuse, neglect or misappropriation of property. The check is printed or saved and placed in the employee file.

For every employee with or who may have resident contact, the Administrator starts the Health Care Worker Background Check Act process and has fingerprints collected electronically and sent to the Illinois State Police within 10 working days. The Administrator follows STF-02 for results and for any disqualifying conviction or waiver.

At hire, before unsupervised resident contact, and at least annually, each employee receives training on recognizing abuse, neglect and exploitation, residents' rights, dementia-related behaviors, and how and where to report. Attendance is recorded and the employee signs an acknowledgment of this policy.

Posted notices in a common area list the Administrator's name and phone, and the current numbers for IDPH, the Department on Aging's Adult Protective Services program, the Senior HelpLine and the Long-Term Care Ombudsman, as maintained by the Administrator in [PHONE LIST LOCATION]. The Administrator checks the numbers every quarter.

Any staff member who sees, suspects or is told of abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately protects the resident. This may mean separating the people involved and getting medical care. The staff member then tells the Administrator or the on-call manager at once. If the Administrator is the person suspected, the staff member calls the authorities directly.
If a resident is in immediate danger or a crime may have occurred, the staff member or manager calls 911 first.

The manager removes the accused staff member from resident contact immediately and keeps them off duty while the investigation continues. If the accused is a resident or visitor, the manager protects other residents and changes supervision as needed.

The Administrator makes the required reports to IDPH, to the Department on Aging's Adult Protective Services program and to law enforcement where a crime is suspected, by phone immediately and in writing as the law requires. The report includes what happened, who was involved, when, and what was done to protect the resident. The Administrator records the time, the person spoken to and any report number.

The Administrator notifies the resident's representative and the designated individual in the contract promptly, and the resident's physician where there is an injury or a change in condition. The Administrator offers the resident the Ombudsman's contact.

The Administrator starts an internal investigation the same day. It includes interviews with the resident, witnesses and the accused, a review of records and schedules, photographs of injuries taken with consent, and preservation of evidence. The Administrator cooperates fully with IDPH, Adult Protective Services and law enforcement, and does not interfere with their investigations.
Staff who are interviewed give written statements before the end of the shift or within 24 hours. No one is to discuss the allegation with other staff or residents except as needed.

The Administrator completes the internal investigation as quickly as possible and documents findings and corrective action. Substantiated abuse, neglect or misappropriation by a certified nurse aide or other registry-eligible person is reported to IDPH for registry action, as required.

Corrective action may include discipline up to termination, retraining, a change in care plans or supervision, and referral to a licensing board. [AGENCY NAME] does not give a positive reference to a former employee who abused, neglected or exploited a resident.

The Administrator reviews the resident's situation after the investigation and updates the service plan and supervision as needed. The resident and representative are told the outcome as far as the law allows.

Staff may not borrow from, sell to, accept gifts or money from, or serve as a power of attorney or beneficiary for any resident. Resident funds are handled only as described in RR-05, and at least two staff members are involved in any cash handling.
All allegations and outcomes are reported to the Quality Improvement Committee every quarter, without resident identifying details beyond what is needed, to find patterns and fix causes. See GOV-04.
Anyone who retaliates against a person who reports in good faith is subject to discipline up to termination.

responsibilities.duty: Protect residents, report suspicions immediately, cooperate with investigations and never retaliate.
Screen staff, ensure training, make required reports, lead the investigation and apply corrective action.
Act for the Administrator after hours, including protecting the resident and removing the accused from duty.
Assess and document the resident's condition and injuries and notify the physician.
Review allegations and outcomes for trends.

documentation: Nurse Aide Registry check results
Background check records and dates fingerprints were sent
Training attendance records and signed policy acknowledgments
Allegation report and investigation file
Reports to IDPH, Adult Protective Services and law enforcement, with date, time and recipient
Notifications to the representative and designated individual
Corrective action records
Quality Improvement Committee review notes

policies.title: Incident and Accident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME]; the Administrator and the Quality Improvement Committee review and report
policies.purpose: To ensure every incident and accident involving a resident is recognized, responded to, reported inside and outside the establishment as required, investigated, and used to prevent it from happening again.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires every staff member to report any incident or accident involving a resident, visitor or staff member, or any near miss, by the end of the shift in which it occurred. The Administrator reviews every report, decides which events must be reported to IDPH and other agencies under the Department's current rules, and makes those reports within the time the rules allow. The Administrator will keep a current list of reportable events, deadlines and report contents taken from the Department's rule text and kept with this policy. Where a rule sets a shorter deadline than this policy, the rule controls. Incident data is fed into the Quality Improvement Program so that causes are found and fixed.

definitions.definition: Any event that is outside routine care and results in, or could result in, harm to a resident, such as a fall, injury, medication error, elopement, resident-to-resident altercation, unexplained injury, fire, or unplanned hospitalization.
An unplanned event that causes or may cause injury or damage.
An event that could have caused harm but did not, such as a medication error caught before it reached the resident.
An incident that the Department's rules or other law require to be reported to IDPH or another agency.
The written form completed by staff that records the facts of an incident.

procedures: The staff member who discovers or witnesses an incident first makes the resident safe and gets emergency help, calling 911 when needed, and stays with the resident.

The staff member tells the Administrator or on-call manager and the nurse immediately by phone. For serious injuries, deaths, elopements, allegations of abuse or neglect, or fires, this call is made at once, at any hour.
The nurse assesses the resident as soon as possible, records vital signs and injuries, and calls the physician if there is an injury or a change in condition. See HCS-04.

The manager notifies the resident's representative and the designated individual under the resident's contract as soon as possible, and no later than [NOTIFICATION DEADLINE IN HOURS] hours after a significant incident. Staff record the time, the person told and what was said.

The staff member who witnessed or discovered the incident completes the incident report before the end of the shift, using facts only, and does not guess at causes. Staff who witnessed it each give a short written statement if asked.
The manager keeps the scene and any equipment involved as it was, where safe, and takes photographs where appropriate with respect for the resident's privacy.
The Administrator reviews each incident report within one business day and decides whether it is a reportable event. This decision, with the reasoning, is noted on the report.

If the event is reportable, the Administrator makes the report to IDPH or the other agency by the required method and within the required deadline, and records the date, time and recipient. Events that also involve suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation follow SAF-01, and deaths follow HCS-09.

The Administrator or nurse starts a review of the cause, including the resident's condition and care plan, staffing, environment, equipment and medications, within three business days for serious incidents.

The nurse updates the resident's service plan and risk measures as needed after the incident, for example falls interventions under HCS-06, and tells staff who care for the resident of the changes before their next shift.
For 72 hours after a serious incident or a fall with injury, staff monitor the resident and record observations on the schedule the nurse sets.
The Administrator follows up on environmental or equipment problems found, by repair order, and records when the problem was fixed. See SAF-10.
The Administrator keeps all incident reports in a confidential incident file, separate from the resident's chart. A summary note is added to the resident's chart without any judgment of fault.

The Administrator compiles incident data monthly by type, location, shift, time of day and resident, and gives it to the Quality Improvement Committee, which uses it to identify trends and set improvement actions. See GOV-04.
The Administrator reviews staff compliance with reporting, and staff who fail to report an incident are counseled and retrained, and may be disciplined if they repeat.
Incident files are retained under REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Make the resident safe, report immediately, and complete an accurate report by the end of the shift.
Assess the resident, notify the physician, and update the service plan.
Review each report, decide and make required external reports, direct the investigation and follow up on corrective actions.
Review trends monthly or quarterly and set prevention actions.

documentation: Incident reports and witness statements
Reportable event decision note
Copies of reports to IDPH or other agencies, with date, time and recipient
Notification log for physician, representative and designated individual
Follow-up monitoring records
Monthly incident summary and Quality Improvement Committee minutes
Maintenance and repair records

policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff of [AGENCY NAME] on every shift, with particular attention to staff serving residents with dementia or other cognitive impairment
policies.purpose: To prevent residents from leaving the establishment unsafely, and to ensure a fast, organized search and response if a resident is missing.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies each resident's risk of wandering or elopement before admission, at each assessment and on any change in condition, and plans supervision to match. Where [AGENCY NAME] offers a special dementia program, it will keep policies that ensure the safety of residents who may wander, and it will tell IDPH and residents about the program as the Act requires. A resident who is missing triggers an immediate search, in which every available staff member takes part, followed by calls to 911 and notifications. Residents keep their right to come and go. Safety measures will be the least restrictive that protect the resident, and will be agreed with the resident or representative where possible. General supervision will be provided as set out in the service plan and the staffing requirements of the Department's rules.

definitions.definition: A resident leaves the building or grounds without staff knowing, when the resident is unable to leave safely.
Aimless or disoriented movement that may place a resident at risk, often related to dementia.
A resident whose location is unknown and who cannot be found in the building or on the grounds after a first check.
A review of a resident's history, cognition, behaviors, mobility and past attempts to leave, used to set supervision and safeguards.
A program that [AGENCY NAME] offers and discloses to IDPH and residents as care specifically for residents with Alzheimer's disease or other dementia.

procedures: During pre-admission screening, the nurse asks about past wandering, exit-seeking, getting lost and prior police or missing-person events, and records the answers. Any dementia-related assessment must use the validated tool and physician (or other qualified practitioner) approval that the Act requires.
At admission, at each reassessment, and whenever there is a change of condition, the nurse completes an elopement risk assessment and records the result in the resident's record.

For residents at risk, the service plan states the specific supervision, such as checks every [CHECK INTERVAL IN MINUTES] minutes, a room close to the nurses' station, structured activities at high-risk times, and any alarm or monitoring device. The plan is developed with the resident or representative and the physician where possible.

With the resident's or representative's consent, the nurse obtains a recent photograph and a physical description, and keeps them in a confidential Missing Resident Packet in the manager's office. The packet also holds the resident's medications, medical conditions, preferred places and the contacts for the family.

Any alarm, door-monitoring device or secured area must be reviewed with the Administrator and checked for compliance with fire and life safety requirements before use. See SAF-06 and SAF-10. Locks that prevent exit during an emergency are never used. See SAF-04.
The staff on each shift receive the names of residents at elopement risk at shift report, and counts are taken at the start of each shift and after meals and activities for those residents.
If a staff member notices a resident is missing, the staff member announces the code [MISSING RESIDENT CODE WORD] right away, and the person in charge takes command.

The person in charge assigns staff to search at once: every room, bathroom, closet, stairwell, common area, vehicles, and the grounds, starting with the places the resident is known to favor. Doors are monitored. Residents are not left unsupervised in order to search.

If the resident is not found within [SEARCH LIMIT IN MINUTES] minutes of the first alert, or at once if the resident is high-risk, vulnerable to weather, or there is any sign of danger, the person in charge calls 911 and gives the description, the time last seen, clothing, and conditions. Extreme heat or cold shortens the time. Staff do not delay a 911 call to continue searching.

The person in charge notifies the Administrator and the nurse, who then notify the resident's representative and physician immediately. The Administrator tells the other agencies required, and handles any media or public enquiries.
Searchers keep in contact by phone or radio, record the areas covered and the times, and a staff member stays at the front desk to guide police, receive information and keep the log.

When the resident is found, staff provide first aid and call EMS if needed. The nurse assesses the resident for injury, dehydration and temperature exposure, and calls the physician. All who were told of the event are called back, and police are told the search is over.
The Administrator completes an incident report and reports to IDPH and others as required, under SAF-02, and treats any event that suggests neglect under SAF-01.

Within 72 hours, the Administrator and nurse review how the resident left and what failed, update the elopement risk assessment and service plan, repair any door, alarm or staffing gap, and tell staff of the change. A resident who leaves repeatedly, and for whom the danger cannot be removed, is reviewed under ADM-04 and ADM-05.
[AGENCY NAME] holds a missing-resident drill at least once every quarter, rotating across shifts. The Administrator records the response time and any problems and corrects them.

In the dementia program, [AGENCY NAME] communicates with the family and designated representative about wandering risk and any events, provides cognitive stimulation and activities that reduce exit-seeking, and trains direct care staff and the Director in dementia care. See HCS-05 and STF-03.

responsibilities.duty: Know which residents are at risk, perform checks, raise the alarm and take part in searches.
Direct the search, call 911 when the criteria are met and keep the log.
Complete elopement risk assessments, update service plans and assess the resident on return.
Maintain the Missing Resident Packets, run drills, report to agencies and fix system failures.

documentation: Elopement risk assessment
Service plan supervision measures
Missing Resident Packet and consent for photograph
Search log and 911 call time
Incident report and external reports
Notification log
Post-event review and service plan update
Missing-resident drill records

policies.title: Restraints and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contractors of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect residents' freedom, dignity and safety by prohibiting restraint and seclusion and by requiring least-restrictive, person-centered responses to behavior and safety risks.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not use physical restraints, chemical restraints or seclusion, and does not use any device, medication or practice to restrict a resident's movement or behavior for staff convenience, discipline or because of staffing levels. This includes tying or holding a resident down, bed rails or chairs used to prevent a resident from getting up, locked rooms and medications given to control behavior rather than to treat a diagnosed condition. Staff may use only the minimum protective action needed in a true emergency to prevent immediate serious harm, and then must call for help. A resident who is a danger to self or others, where the danger cannot be removed by appropriate treatment and services, will be assessed for discharge, and the establishment will not rely on restrictive practices to keep that resident. In the dementia program, safety policies protect residents by supervision, environment and engagement, and not by restraint. [AGENCY NAME] will follow the Department's rules and Illinois law on resident rights and will comply with the Americans with Disabilities Act, including reasonable modifications for residents with disabilities. The Administrator will check the Department's current rules on restraint at least annually and whenever IDPH issues guidance. Where a rule is stricter, the rule controls.

definitions.definition: Any manual method, device, garment, furniture or equipment that restricts a resident's freedom of movement or normal access to the body and that the resident cannot easily remove.
A medication used to control behavior or restrict movement that is not required to treat a resident's diagnosed medical condition.
Involuntary confinement of a resident alone in a room or area from which the resident cannot leave.
Any action or condition that limits a resident's rights, movement or choices, including locked doors, door alarms used to stop exit, and limits on visitors.
The briefest and least forceful action needed to stop immediate serious physical harm while help is on its way, and not a planned intervention.

procedures: Staff do not apply any physical restraint, give any medication to control behavior without a physician's order for a diagnosed condition, or confine any resident in a room. Any staff member who does so is subject to discipline up to termination and may be reported under SAF-01.

When a resident has a safety problem, such as falls, wandering or aggression, the nurse first identifies the cause through assessment, including pain, infection, medication effects, unmet needs, noise and routines, and tries non-restrictive measures such as more supervision, a change in routine, activities, a toileting schedule or a lower bed.
The nurse records the alternatives tried, and the result, in the resident's record and service plan under ADM-03.

A resident who wants to use a device that might limit movement, such as a bed rail for positioning, is assessed by the nurse and physician. The resident's choice, the risks and the safeguards are explained and recorded under a Negotiated Risk Agreement where appropriate. The resident must be able to release the device without help, and the device must not be used to confine. See ADM-06.

Doors, alarms and secured areas are never locked in a way that stops residents from leaving in a fire or emergency. Any device is reviewed with the Administrator for life safety compliance before use. See SAF-06 and SAF-10.

In an emergency, where a resident is about to seriously hurt self or others, staff use verbal de-escalation first, move other residents away, and use the minimum physical contact needed only as long as needed. They call the person in charge and, where there is a risk of serious harm, 911.

After any emergency protective action, the nurse examines the resident for injury and distress within the shift and calls the physician. The staff member completes an incident report before the end of the shift, and the Administrator reviews it under SAF-02 and decides whether it is reportable to IDPH.
The Administrator notifies the resident's representative and designated individual promptly after any such event.

Within three business days, the Administrator and nurse review the event, update the service plan and risk measures, and decide whether the establishment can continue to meet the resident's needs safely.

If the resident is dangerous to self or others and the danger cannot be removed through appropriate treatment and services, or the establishment lacks the skilled staff needed, the Administrator begins retention review and discharge planning under ADM-04 and ADM-05, with the resident's rights to notice and appeal respected. Hospital or behavioral health evaluation is requested where needed.

Residents who take psychotropic medication are reviewed by the nurse and physician on a regular schedule to confirm the medication treats a diagnosed condition, the dose is the lowest effective one, and side effects are monitored. See HCS-01 and HCS-02.
Staff are trained at hire and annually on this policy, on residents' rights, on dementia-related behaviors, and on de-escalation. Training is recorded under STF-03.
In dementia care, staff use redirection, activities, a calm environment and consistent routines, and do not use restraints. See HCS-05.

The Administrator reviews every use of emergency protective action, and any restrictive device, at least quarterly with the Quality Improvement Committee, to confirm that it was needed and to find ways to prevent it. See GOV-04.

Residents with disabilities receive reasonable modifications to this policy and to their environment so that their safety needs are met without unnecessary limits on their independence, as the Americans with Disabilities Act requires.

responsibilities.duty: Never restrain or seclude a resident, use de-escalation, call for help, and report any restraint they see.
Assess causes of unsafe behavior, try alternatives, review medications with the physician and examine the resident after any emergency action.
Enforce the prohibition, review every event, decide on external reports, begin discharge planning where needed and confirm current rules.
Review events and devices and recommend prevention steps.

Service plan and Negotiated Risk Agreement, if any
Incident report for any emergency protective action
Nurse's post-event assessment
Physician notification record
Discharge planning records, if applicable
Training attendance records
Quality Improvement Committee minutes

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan
policies.applies_to: All staff, residents and volunteers; assisted living and shared housing operations, including any special dementia program
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] can protect residents during fires, severe weather, utility failures, infectious disease events and other emergencies. The plan covers sheltering in place, evacuation, relocation, continuity of medications and care, and communication with families and authorities.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan that meets the disaster preparedness requirements of the Illinois Department of Public Health (IDPH) for licensed assisted living and shared housing establishments. The plan is based on a written hazard assessment of this site and this resident population. It is reviewed at least annually and after any activation or drill that reveals a gap. Staffing patterns must allow staff to evacuate or shelter all residents, including residents who cannot move independently to safety. IDPH rule requires sufficient awake staff 24 hours a day for those residents. If [AGENCY NAME] operates a special dementia program, the plan includes emergency procedures and emergency staffing patterns for that program, as required by 210 ILCS 9/150, and wandering and evacuation safety measures. Medication continuity during an emergency follows 210 ILCS 9/70 and the medication policies, with medications administered only by persons authorized under HCS-02. The Administrator confirms the plan content, review frequency and drill frequency against the current IDPH rule text and local requirements, and records the confirmation in the plan binder.

definitions.definition: Keeping residents and staff inside the building, in the safest areas, during an event such as a tornado or hazardous outdoor condition.
Moving residents out of the building or an affected area, either horizontally within the building or to the outside or an off-site location.

A written review of the emergencies most likely to affect this site (for example tornado, flood, winter storm, extreme heat, power outage, fire, water or gas loss, infectious disease outbreak) and the resident needs they would affect.
A current list showing each resident's ability to move to safety, assistive devices, oxygen or equipment needs, cognitive status and the staff assistance required.
A pre-arranged alternate location, supported by a written agreement, where residents can be housed and cared for if the building cannot be occupied.
A program the establishment has disclosed to IDPH and residents as providing care for residents with Alzheimer's disease or other dementias.

procedures: The Administrator completes a written hazard assessment of the site before opening and reviews it at least annually. It addresses local weather hazards, loss of electricity, heat, water or gas, fire, infectious disease events and the specific needs of current residents.

The Administrator writes the Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan and keeps it in a binder at the staff station, with an electronic copy off site. The plan states the chain of command, how an emergency is declared, who is responsible for each task, and who acts if the Administrator is unavailable.

The plan includes procedures for shelter in place, internal (horizontal) movement, full evacuation and relocation. It identifies safe areas for each hazard, exits and routes, equipment for moving non-ambulatory residents, and assembly points.

The Administrator arranges at least one relocation site and transportation resources, with written agreements signed by the receiving party. Agreements are renewed at least annually and kept in the plan binder.

The Director of Resident Services maintains the evacuation capability roster. It is updated within 24 hours of any admission, discharge or change in a resident's mobility, cognition or equipment needs, and at every service plan review. A current copy is kept at the staff station and in the go-kit.

The Administrator sets staffing schedules so that enough awake, trained staff are on duty at all times to move or shelter all residents on the roster, including those who cannot move independently to safety. Each shift's emergency assignments are posted. An on-call list and call-in procedure back up the schedule.

If a special dementia program operates, the plan includes written emergency procedures and staffing patterns for that unit. They cover resident tracking, calming and escort practices, secured-door release during evacuation, and elopement checks after evacuation (see HCS-05 and SAF-03).

The Administrator keeps an emergency supply kit with flashlights, batteries, a battery or hand-crank radio, first aid supplies, resident roster with photos, emergency contacts, and drinking water, food and incontinence supplies for at least [NUMBER OF DAYS] days. The Maintenance Lead checks and restocks the kit monthly and records the check.

The Director of Resident Services keeps medication continuity supplies ready: current medication administration records, resident medication lists and the pharmacy's emergency contact. During an evacuation, medications and records travel with the residents under the control of a staff member authorized under HCS-02.

The Administrator trains all staff on the plan at hire during orientation and at least annually. Training covers each person's role, evacuation methods, resident tracking and how to reach the Administrator. Training is recorded on a sign-in sheet.

The Administrator conducts drills and exercises of the plan at the frequency required by current IDPH rule and local authorities, which the Administrator records on the annual calendar. The drills cover each shift, and at least some are held at night when staffing is lowest. Fire drills follow SAF-06.

When an emergency occurs, the first staff member to recognize it calls 911 if there is a threat to life, then notifies the Administrator or on-call manager. The senior staff member on site acts as Incident Commander until the Administrator arrives.

During an emergency, the Incident Commander assigns staff to account for every resident using the roster, keeps a written log of resident locations, and assigns a staff member to monitor residents with oxygen, dementia or other high needs. Staff do not leave the building or site until all residents are accounted for.

The Administrator notifies family members and resident representatives as soon as it is safe to do so, and no later than [NUMBER] hours after the start of the event. The Administrator also contacts the local emergency management agency and utility companies as needed. IDPH and other reportable notifications follow SAF-02 and REC-02.

If residents are relocated, the Administrator confirms with the receiving site that staffing, medications, diets and equipment can meet each resident's needs. The Administrator records the time, destination and transport method for each resident, and notifies families of the new location.

Before returning residents to the building, the Administrator and Maintenance Lead confirm that utilities, fire protection systems, water, heating and cooling are working and that the building is safe. Where required, the Administrator consults the local fire authority.

Within 14 days after any activation or drill with a problem, the Administrator holds a debrief with staff. The Administrator documents lessons learned and corrective actions, updates the plan, and presents the findings to the quality committee under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Owns the plan; completes the hazard assessment; secures relocation agreements; schedules and confirms drills; reviews the plan annually; ensures staffing supports evacuation; and makes required notifications.
Maintains the evacuation capability roster and medication continuity supplies; ensures resident care needs are met during emergencies; and leads resident accounting.
Maintains emergency supplies, generators or backup power if installed, utilities shut-offs and building safety checks.
Directs response until the Administrator arrives, accounts for all residents and keeps the emergency log.
Know the plan and their assignments, attend training and drills, and follow direction during emergencies.

documentation: Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan with annual review signature and date
Hazard assessment
Evacuation capability roster with update dates
Relocation site and transportation agreements
Drill and exercise records with date, shift, participants, performance and corrective actions
Staff training sign-in sheets
Monthly emergency supply kit checks
Emergency activation log, resident accounting log and family notification record
After-action review and corrective action record

policies.title: Fire Safety, Evacuation and Drills
policies.applies_to: All staff, residents and visitors; assisted living and shared housing operations
policies.purpose: To prevent fires, ensure that fire protection systems work, and make sure every resident can be moved to safety quickly with the staff on duty.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains the building and its fire protection systems in compliance with the physical plant standards in IDPH rules and the Life Safety Code as adopted by IDPH, and with requirements of the local fire authority. Sufficient awake staff must be on duty at all times to evacuate residents who cannot independently move to an area of safety. Each shift must include at least one direct care staff person with current adult CPR certification, including a skills demonstration, as required by 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000. Fire drills, alarm and extinguisher testing, and system inspections are carried out at the frequencies required by current IDPH rule, the Life Safety Code and the local fire authority. The Administrator confirms those frequencies in writing and enters them on the annual safety calendar. Medication and care tasks continue during fire response only as allowed by 210 ILCS 9/70 and by persons authorized under that section.

definitions.definition: A location inside or outside the building that is protected from fire and smoke, such as the outside at an assembly point or a smoke compartment designated by the Life Safety Code.
A planned practice of the fire alarm response and evacuation procedure, conducted and timed with staff and residents as appropriate.
Staff who are on duty, on site and not sleeping, able to respond immediately to an alarm or a resident need.
Rescue residents in immediate danger, Alarm, Contain by closing doors, Extinguish or Evacuate. [AGENCY NAME]'s staff response sequence.
The fire and life safety standards of the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA 101) as adopted by IDPH for these establishments.

procedures: Before licensure, the Administrator coordinates the Life Safety Code survey with the IDPH Design and Construction Section and corrects any deficiency found. The Administrator keeps the approval documents on file.

The Administrator obtains the fire alarm, sprinkler, extinguisher and emergency lighting requirements that apply to this building from IDPH rules, the Life Safety Code and the local fire authority, and enters the required inspection and testing dates on the annual safety calendar.

The Administrator posts evacuation floor plans showing exits, routes, extinguisher and alarm pull station locations and assembly points, on each floor and in each wing. Staff review the maps with residents at move-in.

The Maintenance Lead tests the fire alarm, emergency lighting and extinguishers, and inspects exits and exit signs, at the frequency required. Any deficiency is repaired immediately; if a system is out of service, the Administrator posts a fire watch with awake staff and notifies the fire authority and the alarm company the same day.
The Maintenance Lead keeps exits, corridors and stairways free of obstruction at all times. Staff report blocked exits or propped fire doors to the Maintenance Lead immediately.

Every shift is staffed with at least one awake staff person who holds current adult CPR certification, including a skills demonstration. The Administrator checks CPR expiration dates monthly. The schedule is built so that sufficient awake staff are on duty to evacuate all residents on the evacuation capability roster (see SAF-05).

The Director of Resident Services records each resident's evacuation needs on the roster. These cover mobility device, assistance level, cognitive status, oxygen use and hearing or vision limits. The roster is updated whenever a resident's condition changes and is kept at the staff station.

The Administrator schedules fire drills at the required frequency, on all shifts, at varied times, including at night when staffing is lowest. Drills use the actual alarm and follow the evacuation procedure without alerting residents unnecessarily beyond what is safe.

During a drill, the Administrator or designee records the time of alarm, time each area was cleared, number of residents and staff, resident assistance needed, and problems observed. Any resident who refuses to participate or requires special help is noted in the record.

When an alarm sounds or fire is discovered, staff follow RACE: remove residents in immediate danger, activate the alarm and call 911, close doors, and extinguish only a small fire if trained and safe. Staff then evacuate residents to the area of safety, starting with those closest to the fire.

Staff account for all residents at the assembly point using the roster and report the count to the senior staff member, who tells the fire department immediately about anyone missing. Staff stay with residents, keep them warm and protected from weather, and monitor those with high needs.
Staff take the resident roster, the emergency contact list and the medication records when evacuating if it is safe to do so. Residents do not re-enter the building until the fire department allows.

Smoking, candles, open flames, space heaters and extension cords are controlled under SAF-08 and SAF-10. Cooking areas are monitored whenever in use, and the Dietary Manager ensures staff are trained in the use of kitchen extinguishers.

All new staff receive fire safety training during orientation before working alone, covering alarm locations, RACE, extinguisher use, evacuation methods and resident assignments. Training is repeated at least annually and after any drill that finds a problem.

After any actual fire or drill failure, the Administrator reports the event under SAF-02 and REC-02 as required, reviews performance with staff within 7 days, corrects the problems and brings the results to the quality committee (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures compliance with fire and life safety requirements, schedules drills and inspections, maintains staffing for evacuation, and reports fires and losses.
Tests and maintains alarms, extinguishers, emergency lighting and exits; arranges repairs; and keeps records.
Maintains the evacuation capability roster and ensures resident evacuation needs are addressed in service plans.
Know alarm and evacuation procedures, take part in drills, and respond to alarms using RACE.
Directs response until the Administrator or fire department arrives and conducts resident accounting.

documentation: IDPH Design and Construction Life Safety Code approval documents
Annual safety calendar with required frequencies and Administrator's confirmation
Fire drill records
Fire alarm, sprinkler, extinguisher and emergency lighting inspection and test records
Evacuation floor plans and evacuation capability roster
Fire watch logs
Staff fire safety training records and CPR certification tracking
Incident reports and debrief records

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control
policies.applies_to: All staff, contractors, volunteers, residents and visitors; assisted living and shared housing operations
policies.purpose: To prevent the spread of infection among residents, staff and visitors, to protect employees from bloodborne pathogen exposure, and to detect and respond promptly to outbreaks.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains written infection prevention and control practices and communicable disease policies that satisfy IDPH requirements for these establishments. They are applied consistently to every resident and every employee. Standard precautions are used for all residents at all times, with additional precautions based on the type of infection. Employee exposure to blood and other potentially infectious materials is controlled under the OSHA Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, through a written exposure control plan, hepatitis B vaccination offers, protective equipment and post-exposure follow-up. Reportable diseases and outbreaks are reported to the local health department and IDPH as required by Illinois law. The Administrator verifies current reporting requirements and timeframes with the local health department and records them in the Infection Control Manual. Reporting details are in SAF-09. Staff with signs of communicable illness do not work until cleared under STF-04.

definitions.definition: Basic infection control practices applied to all residents: hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, safe handling of sharps, respiratory etiquette, environmental cleaning and safe handling of laundry and waste.
Additional measures (contact, droplet or airborne) used when a resident has a known or suspected infection that spreads in a particular way.

An increase in cases of an illness above what is expected among residents or staff, such as two or more residents with similar symptoms in a short period, or any number defined as an outbreak by the local health department.
The written plan required by 29 CFR 1910.1030 to identify employees with occupational exposure and to minimize that exposure.
Microorganisms in human blood that can cause disease, including hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV.

procedures: The Administrator designates an Infection Control Coordinator, who is the Director of Resident Services unless another qualified person is named in writing, to oversee this program. The coordinator's name and phone number are posted at the staff station.

The coordinator writes the Infection Control Manual, which includes standard precautions, transmission-based precautions, hand hygiene, cleaning and disinfection, laundry, waste and sharps handling, food safety, and illness reporting. The coordinator reviews it at least annually and after any outbreak.

All staff are trained at hire and at least annually on standard precautions, hand hygiene, use of protective equipment, cleaning of blood and body fluids, and when to report symptoms. Training is documented on a sign-in sheet and in the personnel file.

Staff perform hand hygiene before and after resident contact, before handling food or medications, after glove removal and after using the restroom. Alcohol-based hand rub and handwashing supplies are available at care locations; the Maintenance Lead checks supplies weekly.

The coordinator ensures that gloves, gowns, masks, eye protection and disinfectants are stocked. Housekeeping uses disinfectants appropriate to the pathogen, on high-touch surfaces at least daily and as often as needed, and on bathrooms and shared equipment after each use.

Employees with occupational exposure are offered hepatitis B vaccination at no cost within 10 working days of assignment, in accordance with 29 CFR 1910.1030. The offer is recorded, and a signed declination is kept if the vaccine is refused.

The Administrator maintains the written bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan, reviews it annually, and provides labeled sharps containers, biohazard bags and protective equipment. Staff do not recap used needles and place sharps in containers immediately after use.

If an employee has a needlestick or other exposure, the employee washes the area, tells the supervisor immediately, and is sent for medical evaluation as soon as possible. The Administrator documents the incident and follow-up, keeps the medical information confidential, and reviews whether controls need improvement.

When a resident shows signs of infection (fever, new cough, vomiting, diarrhea, rash, wound drainage, or urinary symptoms), staff tell the nurse or Director of Resident Services right away. The nurse assesses the resident, notifies the physician under HCS-04, and starts precautions as directed by the Infection Control Manual.

The coordinator keeps a monthly infection log listing each resident infection, date of onset, symptoms, type, treatment and outcome, and reviews it for patterns. The log is brought to the quality committee under GOV-04.

If two or more residents or staff develop similar symptoms within a short time, the coordinator notifies the Administrator immediately, begins outbreak precautions, and contacts the local health department. Reports to the local health department and IDPH are made as required by law, and the coordinator records the contact, name of the person spoken to and instructions given.

During an outbreak, the Administrator may restrict group activities, communal dining or visitation to the extent necessary and as directed by public health authorities. Restrictions are limited to what is needed, are communicated to residents, representatives and families, and do not remove residents' rights under RR-01 and RR-10.
Staff who have vomiting, diarrhea, fever, rash of unknown cause, or other signs of communicable disease report to the supervisor before the shift and are excluded from work in accordance with STF-04.
Food handlers follow safe food handling practices under DL-01. Housekeeping and laundry staff follow DL-03 for handling soiled linen and waste.

Residents are offered influenza, pneumococcal, COVID-19 and other recommended vaccines through their physician or pharmacy. Vaccination offers, acceptances and declinations are documented in the resident record.

The Administrator evaluates the program at least annually, including infection logs, staff compliance observations and outbreak response, and records corrective actions in the quality improvement record.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures the program is funded and implemented, makes or confirms outbreak notifications, and maintains the exposure control plan.
Writes and updates the manual, trains staff, keeps the infection log, leads outbreak response and reports to the quality committee.
Assesses residents with symptoms, notifies physicians and implements precautions.
Clean and disinfect, handle linen and waste safely and report supply needs.
Practice standard precautions, report symptoms in themselves and residents, and use protective equipment.

documentation: Infection Control Manual with annual review date
Bloodborne pathogen exposure control plan
Hepatitis B vaccine offer and declination forms
Staff infection control training records
Monthly infection log
Outbreak investigation and reporting records
Exposure incident reports and follow-up
Resident vaccination records

policies.title: Smoking, Visitors and Pets
policies.applies_to: All residents, staff, visitors and volunteers; assisted living and shared housing operations
policies.purpose: To protect residents' rights to visitors, to keep residents and staff safe from fire and smoke, and to allow pets in a way that protects residents' health and safety.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects each resident's right to receive visitors. Visitor access is subject to resident rights and the essential support person provisions of Illinois law and rules. Restrictions on visitors are limited to what is needed to protect resident safety, other residents' rights, or public health, and are never used as punishment. Smoking is governed by applicable Illinois law, local ordinances and the establishment's written smoking policy. The Administrator confirms the current requirements and records them in the smoking policy statement given to residents before move-in. Pets are allowed only as set out in this policy and the establishment contract, in a way that does not endanger residents, and subject to local animal ordinances. Service animals are permitted as required by federal and state law.

definitions.definition: Any person who comes to see a resident who is not an employee, contractor or volunteer.
A person designated by or for a resident to provide in-person support that is necessary for the resident's physical or emotional well-being, whose access must be allowed as described in RR-10.
An outdoor location, if the establishment allows smoking at all, that is away from entrances, windows and air intakes as required by law and the establishment's written policy.
A dog or other animal trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, as defined under the ADA and applicable state law.
An animal kept by a resident in the resident's unit with the Administrator's approval.

procedures: The Administrator states the visiting hours, check-in procedure and rules in the resident handbook. Residents are told that they may receive visitors of their choosing, at any reasonable hour, and in private, and that the hours are guidelines and not a limit on essential support persons or on end-of-life visits.

Front desk or on-duty staff greet each visitor, ask them to sign in with name, time and resident visited, and direct them to the resident. Staff do not require a visitor to state the purpose of the visit unless needed for safety.

Staff ask a resident whether they wish to see a visitor before escorting the visitor to the unit. A resident who declines a visit is not forced to meet the visitor, and the declination is recorded in the visitor log.

The Administrator may limit or end a visit only when the visitor poses a threat to safety, interferes with the care or rights of others, is impaired or violent, or when public health authorities require limits. The staff member documents the reason, the time and the person who made the decision, and tells the resident and representative.

When a resident has an essential support person, staff follow RR-10 and allow access, including when visitation is otherwise limited, subject to reasonable infection control conditions that are applied equally.

If a visitor is suspected of abusing, neglecting or exploiting a resident, staff follow SAF-01, protect the resident, and the Administrator decides whether to restrict contact in consultation with the resident or representative and, where appropriate, law enforcement.

Before move-in, the Administrator gives each resident the written smoking policy. If smoking is allowed, it may occur only in a designated outdoor smoking area that complies with state law and local ordinance. Smoking inside the building, including in resident units, is not allowed. [AGENCY NAME] provides the resident's written notice of this rule at admission.

The service plan team assesses the safety of any resident who smokes, including cognitive status, ability to handle lighters and matches, oxygen use and fire risk. Findings and supervision needs are recorded in the service plan under ADM-03. Where risk is high, a negotiated risk agreement under ADM-06 may be used.
Residents who use oxygen are not permitted to smoke, and no one may smoke within the distance of oxygen use required by the oxygen supplier. Staff post oxygen warning signs on the unit door.

Staff keep lighters and matches of residents who cannot safely manage them in a secured place if the service plan so directs, and Maintenance empties and checks the designated smoking area's receptacles at least daily.

Pets owned by residents are allowed only with the Administrator's prior written approval. The resident must show vaccination records, local license where required, and provide a written plan for feeding, exercise, waste, and care if the resident is hospitalized or unable to care for the pet. A pet agreement is signed and added to the resident record.

The Administrator denies or revokes approval for a pet that is aggressive, causes damage or poses a health or safety risk to others, after notice to the resident and a chance to correct the problem. Residents with allergies or fear of animals are consulted before a pet is approved.

Staff are not required to provide routine care of resident pets unless stated in the service plan and the contract. Pet waste is disposed of promptly and animals are kept out of food preparation areas.

Service animals are allowed anywhere residents are allowed, and staff do not ask for documentation. Staff may ask only if the animal is required because of a disability and what task it performs. A service animal may be removed only if it is out of control and the handler does not take effective action, or it is not housebroken.

Facility-owned animals or therapy animal visits are allowed only if the animals are healthy, vaccinated and supervised, are kept out of kitchens and clean areas, and the Activities Director records the visit. Residents may opt out of contact.
The Administrator reviews visitor, smoking and pet issues, complaints and incidents at least quarterly and updates this policy as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Sets visiting and smoking rules in line with law, approves pets, decides on restrictions and ensures staff follow resident rights.
Assesses smoking and fire risk, includes needs in the service plan and coordinates essential support persons.
Greet visitors, keep the visitor log, ask residents about visitors and report concerns.
Maintains the smoking area and fire safety equipment and posts required signs.
Coordinates approved animal visits and ensures residents can opt out.

documentation: Visitor log and records of any visit restriction with reasons
Written smoking policy acknowledgment signed by residents
Smoking and fire risk assessment in the service plan
Pet agreement, vaccination records and Administrator approval or denial
Records of service animal handling issues
Animal visit records

policies.title: Communicable Disease Reporting and Tuberculin Screening Procedures
policies.applies_to: All employees, residents, Administrator and nursing or health staff; assisted living and shared housing operations
policies.purpose: To ensure that reportable communicable diseases are identified and reported to public health authorities, and that employees and residents are screened for tuberculosis according to IDPH rules.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows IDPH rules on communicable disease policies and tuberculin skin test procedures for assisted living and shared housing establishments. The Administrator verifies the current rule text and the local health department's reporting requirements, lists them in the Infection Control Manual, and keeps the list current. Under 77 Ill. Adm. Code 295.3000, each employee file must contain documentation that the employee is free of pulmonary tuberculosis. Employees do not begin direct resident contact until that documentation is on file. Residents are screened for tuberculosis in accordance with IDPH rule and this policy as part of admission. Reportable diseases, suspected outbreaks and unusual disease occurrences are reported to the local health department and IDPH as required. Employee exposure to bloodborne pathogens is handled under 29 CFR 1910.1030 and SAF-07. Medical information about employees and residents is kept confidential and is shared only as the law allows.

definitions.definition: A disease or condition that Illinois law or the local health department requires health care providers and facilities to report.
A skin test, or an approved blood test (IGRA), used to detect infection with tuberculosis bacteria.
Documentation, such as a negative test result or, for a positive test, a chest X-ray and clinician statement, showing the person does not have active pulmonary tuberculosis.
A cluster of cases of an illness above the expected level, as described in SAF-07 or defined by the local health department.
The person designated by the Administrator to lead the infection prevention program.

procedures: The Administrator obtains the current IDPH rule text on communicable disease policies and tuberculin skin test procedures, and the current list of reportable diseases and reporting timeframes from the local health department. The Administrator records the date of this verification and the sources in the Infection Control Manual and reviews it at least annually.
